item.content:encoded:
Former Los Angeles Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas, who retired after the team fell in the NLCS this season, spoke about the impact his time with the Dodgers had on him.
Rojas is currently serving as a correspondent at the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, but also spared some time before the game to answer questions about himself.
“I told the players, the staff and the front office, not just thank you, they changed my life,” Rojas said. “They got me the opportunity to come back home to LA where I made my debut 12 years ago in 2014 and having the opportunity to live the best four years of my life in baseball.
“It wasn’t just for me, it was for my family, the people that I really care about. My son, they grabbed my son under their wing and they made growth with him. He was shagging balls in the outfield, he was living the dream. …That’s what I told the guys, thank you for changing my life.”
Rojas has sung the Dodgers’ praises the entire year, especially following his retirement. After his last game, the veteran expressed his desire to continue serving the team after stepping away from the sport.
“I want to stay here,” Rojas said. “I want to wear this uniform in a different capacity and continue to make the organization better.”
When Did Miguel Rojas Return to the Dodgers?
Rojas made his debut with the Dodgers in 2014, but the team traded him after his rookie year in a big deal with the Miami Marlins—during which the team also acquired Kiké Hernandez and Austin Barnes.
He stayed with the Marlins for nearly a decade, but the Dodgers decided to bring him back to the team in 2023, sending a minor-league infielder the other way.
Through his 446 games with the team from 2023-26, Rojas hit 22 homers and drove in 117 RBIs for the Dodgers, also posting a .688 OPS and hitting the biggest home run of his life. He stepped up to the plate in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series and hit a solo home run in the top of the ninth to tie the game and swing the momentum in the Dodgers’ favor as they went on to win their second consecutive World Series.
Rojas will forever be a Dodgers legend, and his constant praise of the organization shows how well the team treats their players.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are entering a transitionary period this offseason, with a list of nine potential free agents that includes Alex Vesia among them.
Facing an uncertain future, the left-handed reliever took to Instagram to thank his teammates and fans for their support this season and over the past six years.
Vesia improved upon his 2025 season despite a regression in WHIP, walk rate and strikeout rate. He accomplished this thanks to a lower batting average against and cutting his home runs allowed by over half. That all came while attempting to move past personal tragedy for his family.
The 30-year-old was an important contributor to a Dodgers bullpen that finished in the top five in ERA.
He became one of L.A.’s most trusted relievers since joining the organization in 2021. Vesia has finished with a 2.64 ERA or lower in four of his six seasons with the Dodgers and posted a 2.87 ERA overall during that span.
A reunion makes sense for both sides, but is complicated by the future of the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and the current state of the Dodgers’ roster.
The current CBA expires at 9 p.m. PT on Dec. 1. Players can sign new contracts prior to that point, but will be prohibited from doing so during an expected lockout that will likely drag well into 2027.
As for the Dodgers’ chances of re-signing Vesia, it could depend heavily on how his market develops. The organization is not likely to add another expensive bullpen contract with so much money invested in the group already.
An additional factor working against a reunion is how adept the front office is at identifying reliever talent. The Dodgers can allocate resources elsewhere if they can find a cheaper alternative.
Kiké Hernández’s posts potential goodbye to Dodgers fans
News of Miguel Rojas’ retirement leaves the Dodgers with eight decisions to make regarding potential free agents, one of which is Kiké Hernández.
Like Vesia, Hernández also took to social media to reflect on his time with the Dodgers.
The 35-year-old was open about his wish to re-sign with L.A. once again, but the chances of a deal materializing is not guaranteed.
The Dodgers’ other free agents this offseason include Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Tarik Skubal, and Blake Treinen.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Friedman Hopes Miguel Rojas Will Remain with Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Miguel Rojas may have played his final game in a Dodgers uniform, but Andrew Friedman hopes his association with the organization is far from over.
During Wednesday’s season-ending press conference, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations praised the veteran infielder, who announced his retirement following the team’s elimination from the National League Championship Series against Milwaukee.
Rojas had expressed his desire to remain with the Dodgers in some capacity, and Friedman made it clear that the feeling is mutual.
“Miggy Ro has been awesome,” Friedman said. “Just his impact, not just on the field and the role he played.”
Rojas’s value to the Dodgers has extended well beyond his contributions at the plate or in the field. Over the past several seasons, he has become one of the organization’s most respected clubhouse leaders, serving as a mentor to both established veterans and young players trying to find their footing in the major leagues.
A Lasting Influence on Mookie Betts
Friedman specifically highlighted the role Rojas played in helping Mookie Betts make the difficult transition from right field to shortstop.
“Mookie’s ascension to the shortstop position, and not just being passable but being an above-average defender at short, Miggy Ro’s got his fingerprints around a lot of that,” Friedman explained.
It’s a significant compliment. Betts’s ability to reinvent himself defensively has been one of the more remarkable developments of his Dodgers career, and Rojas was instrumental in helping him learn the finer points of one of baseball’s most demanding positions.
Friedman also credited Rojas with mentoring young infielder Alex Freeland and helping establish the culture that has made the Dodgers so successful.
Those contributions aren’t necessarily reflected in the box scores, but they help explain why the organization values Rojas so highly.
A Career Comes Full Circle
Friedman also reflected on the unusual history he shares with Rojas.
“It’s funny because it was one of the first moves I did when I got here, was trading Miggy Ro away,” Friedman recalled.
Indeed, shortly after Friedman arrived in Los Angeles following the 2014 season, the Dodgers traded Rojas to the Miami Marlins as part of the deal that brought Kiké Hernández and other players to Los Angeles.
Eight years later, Rojas returned to the Dodgers, eventually becoming an important part of the teams that won back-to-back World Series championships in 2024 and 2025.
For Friedman, there was something particularly satisfying about seeing Rojas finish his playing career where it began.
“To kind of bookend his career and have him have a chance to come back and be such a big part of those two championship teams, and for him to go out the way he did, leaving everything on the field, can’t say enough about the guy, the competitor, the teammate,” Friedman said.
A New Role in Los Angeles?
Although Friedman didn’t announce any formal plans for Rojas, he expressed hope that the veteran would continue contributing to the organization.
“We’re hopeful that he’s impacting us in the future as well,” he said.
Given his experience, baseball knowledge and established relationships throughout the clubhouse, Rojas would seem like a natural candidate for a coaching, player development or advisory role.
His retirement closes an important chapter in Dodgers history, particularly for a team that has relied heavily on veteran leadership throughout its championship run.
But if Friedman gets his wish, Rojas will remain part of the Dodgers family.
And after everything he has contributed to the organization, that would be a fitting next chapter for one of the team’s most respected players.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Skubal & Kiké Headlight Dodgers 2027 Free Agent Class
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers.
After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season.
While the list reads as nine, it is essentially eight, as veteran infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers’ Game Four loss.
Free Agents
(9): Blake Treinen, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Alex Vesia, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Tarik Skubal
Blake Treinen
Veteran right-hander Blake Treinen’s season ended during the final week of September after a right shoulder setback that forced him off the Dodgers postseason roster.
Treinen returned to Los Angeles after his 2024 World Series heroics on a 2-year, $14 million contract, and now the 38-year-old will be without a home entering an offseason that may be the final season of his career.
Evan Phillips
Right-hander Evan Phillips missed all of 2025 and returned toward the middle of the 2026 regular season due to Tommy John surgery. However, in his games played, he was very effective, going 3-2 with a 3.46 ERA.
Still, Phillips will be entering his age 33 season and has already missed significant time due to right elbow/arm injuries, and with multiple pitchers in the pipeline, it’s not hard to see the Dodgers moving on.
Kris Bubic
Acquired at the trade deadline, left-hander Kris Bubic is likely to get a contract this Winter as a starter, since that was his primary role before injuries derailed his 2026 season.
Bubic was an All-Star in 2025 and, with a thin free-agent market, could land a nice contract from a team desperate for starting pitching.
Miguel Rojas
Shortly after the conclusion of Game Four of the NLCS, veteran utility infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball, bringing an end to his 13-year playing career.
Rojas is expected to remain with the Dodgers organization in a player devleopment/coaching role.
Kiké Hernández
October hero Kiké Hernández is hitting free agency yet again this Winter, and after a subpar performance in October, minus one huge home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS, not much is known about whether the Dodgers will try to run it back for another 1-year deal.
Overall, Hernández missed most of the season while recovering from elbow surgery and an oblique injury and hit 4 home runs in 90 at-bats while posting a below-average 82 OPS+.
The fan favorite will enter his age-36 season, likely ending his Dodgers tenure for the second time.
Alex Vesia
Arguably the biggest free agent from the Dodgers bullpen this Winter is left-hander Alex Vesia, who has likely pitched his way to a sizable multi-year contract that the Dodgers might not be inclined to match.
Vesia, 30, posted an elite 2.64 ERA and struck out 74 batters despite a below-average fastball velocity, but with backend pitching at a premium, his market is likely to be heavy.
Brusdar Graterol
Brusdar Graterol’s career has been defined by injuries, and that likely will force his time in Dodger Blue to come to an end this Winter.
Despite a 2.78 career ERA, the right-hander has pitched only 7.1 innings for the Dodgers since the 2024 regular season, missing the entire 2025 and 2026 seasons due to right shoulder surgery.
Eric Lauer
Like Bubic, left-hander Eric Lauer will enter the market as a starting pitcher, and after a second-half renaissance with the Dodgers, where he went 7-2 with a 4.50 ERA, he could be a dependable backend starter to eat innings for a variety of clubs.
Tarik Skubal
The consensus No. 1 free agent this Winter across baseball is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is set to demand a massive multi-year contract that could go north of $400 million.
While the Dodgers will no doubt be involved, it’s hard to imagine them matching that while already having so many long-term deals tied up, especially in their starting rotation already.
Skubal is likely to sign before the MLB lockout on December 1st to maximize his contract, such as fellow Scott Boras client Corey Seager did after the 2021 season.

item.content:encoded:
During Spring Training, Hyeseong Kim was in the running to be the Los Angeles Dodgers’ starting second baseman while Tommy Edman was out. Instead, the job went to Alex Freeland.
Kim opened the year in Triple-A and didn’t spend much time with the Dodgers. He appeared in just 43 games and didn’t produce much when given the opportunity.
Kim hit just .259/.323/.328 with one home run, 16 runs scored, 11 RBI, five stolen bases and an 83 wRC+. In the Minors, he wasn’t much better either, slashing .262/.330/.345 with a 77 wRC+ in the hitter-friendly Pacific Coast League.
After a poor season, Kim shared a message on Instagram apologizing for his struggles on the field, thanking fans and the Dodgers for their support, and committing to be better in 2027.
Hello, this is Hyeseong Kim!
Looking back on this season, I’m sorry I couldn’t show you better performances, and I was deeply disappointed in myself as well. Still, I sincerely thank everyone who supported me through it all.
I love the Dodgers, and I have never once been disappointed in this team. It was my choice, and I haven’t regretted it for a single moment. My only disappointment was in myself. I have nothing but gratitude for the team and all the Dodgers fans!
Next year, I will strive to become a better person and a better baseball player. Thank you!😊👍
Kim enters an important year for both his future with the Dodgers and potentially his MLB career. The 2027 season is the final year of his three-year, $12.5 million contract before the Dodgers have club options in 2028 and 2029.
The Dodgers would certainly move on with another poor season from Kim, and there’s no guarantee he even makes it through the offseason in the organization.
If he hits like he did in 2026, other organizations may also just view him as just Minor League depth, putting a lot of pressure on him heading into the new season.
However, the Dodgers have open spots on their bench with Miguel Rojas retiring and Kiké Hernández reaching free agency with the club likely to move on. The additional roster spots could bode well for Kim’s chances of sticking around.
The Dodgers also need to get younger, and Kim will be just 28 years old entering the 2027 season. In addition, he provides a speed element to the roster that no one else does.
Kim’s ability to play the middle infield could also help his chances of sticking around with the Dodgers losing two infielders who served bench roles, but he would also compete with Freeland once again for that role.
But even with his speed and defensive ability, Kim still needs to hit to be on a Major League roster, and his production from 2026 won’t cut it.
In 2025, Kim was still a below-league-average hitter, but he had the benefit of the doubt after moving from South Korea to the United States and facing tougher competition. Now, Kim doesn’t have any excuses, and it’ll be up to him to prove himself as a Major Leaguer.
Dodgers working with Hyeseong Kim’s swing mechanics
Since signing Kim, the Dodgers have been working on his swing mechanics to develop more consistency and pop. That has been ongoing for two seasons now, and they believed his mechanics were the cause of some of his 2026 struggles.
An offseason of working on his swing and resetting could prove beneficial, but with the impending lockout, Kim will not be able to work with Dodgers hitting coaches once it begins, adding another obstacle.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers made one of the most anticipated moves of 2026 ahead of the trade deadline by trading for two-time Cy Young award winner Tarik Skubal, the ace of the Detroit Tigers.
Since Skubal was traded on an expiring contract, there is no guarantee that he will be back on the Dodgers in 2027. LA has been predicted to compete with six teams that would potentially offer the southpaw a deal this offseason — one that is expected to potentially exceed $400 million.
Skubal spoke after last week's postseason exit on what it meant to play for the Dodgers this summer, and though it is no indication of what the financial side of things will look like this offseason, provided a glowing review on the organization.
“I mean, incredible organization, incredible teammates, incredible fanbase,” Skubal said. “Honored to wear the LA across your chest and on the hat. Doesn’t make this feel any better. It sucks, but I think everybody in here gave it everything they had, and sometimes that’s just baseball."
Skubal made 10 regular season starts after the trade and totaled a 2.61 ERA in that span. Over 11 postseason innings (two starts), he had a 2.45 ERA, throwing 14 strikeouts to four walks.
In other news, veteran utility star Kiké Hernández recently spoke on his future as he becomes a free agent once again this offseason. The fan favorite made his intentions known when speaking to reporters after last week's National League Championship Series elimination.
"I would love to have one more try, trying to win another one," Hernández said. "But I don't really know what's going to happen. I hope I'm back, and if I'm not, I hope that I get to play for a winning team."
Finally, among the many free agents on the team, there is one that the Dodgers simply can't afford to lose. Alternatively, there is also one that, according to the team at Dodgers On SI, LA can afford to let walk.

item.content:encoded:
Kiké Hernandez may have played his final game with the Dodgers.
The fan favorite acknowledged the uncertain future he faces as he enters free agency in an Instagram post in which Hernandez expressed his gratefulness for fans.
“LA, we fell short of our big goal. But looking at the big picture, what a ride these last three years were!!” Hernandez wrote in the Instagram caption.
“If this is it for us…. Once again, I will always be thankful for you guys & I will forever love ya! ♾️ #JustAKidFromPR,” Hernandez said.
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman brought Hernandez back on a one-year deal last offseason, saying the “door was always open” for the utilityman. It remains unclear whether that will be the case this winter as Hernandez hits free agency again.
Hernandez has built his career as an electric personality in the Dodgers’ dugout and a clutch bat every October. His postseason numbers are simply mystifying with Hernandez coming to life every fall.
But as the Dodgers look to get younger, the front office may go in another direction this offseason. The Dodgers assembled the most expensive roster in baseball, which also happened to be the oldest.
While the Dodgers won 100 regular-season games with their veteran core, the back-to-back World Series champions were swept by a hungrier, younger Brewers team.
The four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series may alter the Dodgers’ plans as the front office attempts to build another winning roster.
Only time will tell whether Hernandez is a part of that group.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES - La temporada baja ha llegado antes de lo previsto para los Dodgers.
Antes de haber asimilado por completo la derrota del jueves por la noche (6-4) ante los Cerveceros en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —resultado que puso fin a su temporada y a su intento de lograr un tercer título consecutivo—, los Dodgers tuvieron que afrontar la realidad de que probablemente se avecinan cambios en el equipo.
Los Dodgers perderán a nueve jugadores debido a la agencia libre, un grupo encabezado por la figura más destacada del mercado, Tarik Skubal. Los otros jugadores que pronto serán agentes libres son el venezolano Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Eric Lauer, Kris Bubic y el venezolano Brusdar Graterol.
Gran parte del núcleo del equipo de Los Ángeles permanecerá intacto en el futuro previsible, por lo que la ventana competitiva no se está cerrando; sin embargo, este podría ser un periodo de transición entre una era del béisbol de los Dodgers y otra.
"Nunca puedes pensar que este es el final", dijo Rojas, quien permanecerá en la organización desempeñando un papel en el desarrollo de jugadores. "Y conozco muy bien a esta organización; no se conformarán con esta derrota".
A lo largo de 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, los Dodgers han encontrado formas fluidas de incorporar talento joven a sus plantillas para complementar a su núcleo de veteranos experimentados. Ese proceso ya ha comenzado con el dominicano Josue De Paula —el prospecto número 4 a nivel general según MLB Pipeline—, así como con el receptor suplente Dalton Rushing y el jugador de cuadro Alex Freeland.
No obstante, es posible que los Dodgers deban adoptar un enfoque más deliberado para asignar roles más destacados a sus jugadores jóvenes de cara al futuro, lo que dará lugar a decisiones interesantes durante esta temporada baja.
"No conocemos el futuro", comentó el dominicano Teóscar Hernández. "Pero algo que sabemos es que nos preocupamos los unos por los otros, nos cuidamos mutuamente y nos apoyamos durante todo el año... Este grupo es realmente especial, no por lo que hemos logrado en los últimos dos años y en este, sino simplemente por la unión que tenemos".
A continuación, un vistazo a algunas de las decisiones más importantes sobre el roster que deberán tomar los Dodgers durante esta temporada baja:
¿Participarán en la puja por Skubal?
Los Dodgers se desprendieron de dos prospectos clasificados entre los 100 mejores —el abridor listo para las Grandes Ligas River Ryan y el jardinero Zyhir Hope—, además del lanzador derecho Brady Smith, a cambio de contar con Skubal por un periodo de hasta tres meses. No fueron el único equipo dispuesto a hacer una gran inversión por un talento del calibre de Skubal, y lo mismo ocurrirá cuando este llegue al mercado de agentes libres por primera vez.
Skubal ganó su caso de arbitraje salarial contra los Tigres la temporada baja pasada, obteniendo un salario récord de US$32 millones. Se espera ampliamente que consiga la mayor cantidad de dinero garantizado jamás otorgada a un lanzador en la agencia libre, superando el contrato de 12 años y US$325 millones de Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
En su año previo a la agencia libre, Skubal se perdió seis semanas tras someterse a una cirugía en el codo izquierdo, pero aun así completó otra campaña sólida, registrando una marca de 12-7 y una efectividad de 2.72 en 26 aperturas con los Tigres y los Dodgers. Prefirió no hablar sobre su futuro inmediatamente después de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional (SCLN).
"Sí, realmente no voy a hacer comentarios sobre mi futuro", dijo Skubal. "El día de hoy es una porquería, ya sabes, y en eso es en lo que estoy pensando ahora mismo".
Aun así, Skubal expresó su agradecimiento por el tiempo que pasó con los Dodgers.
"Una organización increíble, compañeros increíbles, una afición increíble", dijo. "Es un honor llevar las letras 'L.A.' en el pecho y en la gorra".
¿Cómo le darán tiempo de juego para De Paula?
En septiembre, De Paula hizo que el salto de Doble-A a las Grandes Ligas pareciera sencillo, impresionando tanto a los Dodgers que logró entrar en el roster de postemporada como opción de bateador emergente. Sin embargo, su limitación radicaba en que el equipo de Grandes Ligas lo veía únicamente como bateador designado, una posición ocupada por Shohei Ohtani.
"Creo que la mejora que Josue mostró en los jardines entre 2025 y 2026 es real", comentó el mes pasado Andrew Friedman, presidente de operaciones de béisbol. "Y para nosotros, se trata de dar otro gran paso de cara a 2027. Él tiene las herramientas y la capacidad para lograrlo".
Con el tiempo, los Dodgers tendrán que poner a De Paula a jugar en los jardines. No obstante, sus jardineros titulares —Teóscar Hernández, el cubano Andy Pages y Kyle Tucker— tienen contrato vigente hasta la próxima temporada.
Si los Dodgers consideran que De Paula está listo para ser jugador titular habitual, eso probablemente implicaría, como mínimo, limitar el tiempo de juego de Hernández. También podría darse una medida más drástica: buscar un equipo interesado en asumir la última temporada garantizada de su contrato de tres años y US$66 millones.
Otra opción sería que De Paula comenzara la temporada en Triple-A, donde podría trabajar en su defensa en un entorno de menor presión.
¿Qué jugadores veteranos clave regresarán?
Entre los agentes libres inminentes, algunas de las bajas más significativas en cuanto a liderazgo serían Kiké Hernández, Phillips, Vesia y Treinen. El bullpen ciertamente podría tener hueco para lanzadores de situaciones críticas como Phillips y Vesia, pero el encaje de Hernández entre los jugadores de posición no está tan claro.
Hernández, el propio "Mr. October" de los Dodgers, tuvo una temporada regular marcada por las lesiones. Tampoco estuvo a la altura de su habitual rendimiento en postemporada, conectando apenas un jonrón solitario en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional (SDLN) como único imparable. Es una figura importante en el vestuario y, aunque le encantaría volver a Los Ángeles, sabe que sus necesidades y las del equipo deben coincidir durante la agencia libre.
"Me encantaría intentarlo una vez más, tratar de ganar otro", dijo Hernández. "Pero realmente no sé qué va a pasar. Espero volver y, si no es así, espero poder jugar en un equipo ganador".

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers 2026 report card: Shohei Ohtani gets an F, only two hitters receive an A
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers. In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster. First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in th
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers.
In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster.
First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in the NLCS.
Shohei Ohtani: F
To be clear: The two-way star was the second-best player in the National League this year, hitting 30 home runs and posting a sub-2.00 ERA in 14 starts on the mound. Even in a relatively down year for him, he finished fifth in the majors in Fangraphs’ version of wins above replacement. He remains, undoubtedly, MLB’s foremost star player and the Dodgers’ most potent weapon.
But that is why the way his season finished was such a failure.
What mattered most for the Dodgers this year was having Ohtani –– especially as a hitter –– at full strength come the postseason. By trying to play through right arm and left knee injuries, he wasn’t.
And while there is blame to be shared for the way his health was managed, from team decision-makers to Ohtani himself, it is impossible not to second-guess what this October might have looked like if the slugger was in a better place physically.
Instead, his .192 playoff batting average was not nearly enough to save the Dodgers’ offense. In the end, his one big swing in Game 4 of the NLCS was too little, too late. Moving forward, he and the team might have to reimagine his usage to avoid a repeat of this year. Because, especially as the rest of the roster gets older, they can’t afford another late-season injury crisis like this with Ohtani again.
Freddie Freeman: B-
In his 17th MLB season, Freeman earned his 10th career All-Star selection, finished 13th in the majors in total hits, and continued his march towards Cooperstown. But, the 37-year-old also saw his total production (measured by WAR) decline for a fourth-straight year.
He hit just one regular-season home run after July 4. His batting average dropped from .306 to .288 amid a knee issue in September. And despite a couple big swings in the playoffs, he finished October just 5-for-29. Now, entering the final season of his contract but intending to play at least a couple more beyond that, the Dodgers will have to start deciding if he will remain in their longer-term plans.
Mookie Betts: B
What was shaping up to be a lost year for Betts instead finished with signs of renewed life. On Aug. 4, he was hitting .223 with a .670 OPS. In 46 games after that, he posted a .315/.399/.562 slash line while nearly doubling his home run total from 13 to 23.
It was the best he had looked since the first half of 2024 and a reminder that, even at 34 years old now, there is a superstar level he is still capable of reaching. The Dodgers will be hoping that’s what they get from him in 2027.
Max Muncy: B+
This was a resurgent season for Muncy, who returned to the All-Star Game for the first time since 2021 while hitting for his highest average (.252) since 2018. He stayed healthy, playing 149 games and hitting 29 home runs.
He also improved his defense, earning a nod as a Gold Glove finalist at third base. He’ll be back at third next season, in the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Andy Pages: A-
Pages didn’t sustain his torrid pace from early in the year (he had a .303 average and .899 OPS on May 27, then a .254 average and .751 OPS thereafter) but still cemented himself as the youngest core piece of the roster, earning an All-Star nod with his improved approach and stellar center-field defense. His postseason was an improvement from 2025 too.
Teoscar Hernández: C
A late surge at the plate helped save some of Hernández’s season-long numbers (.267 average, .759 OPS) following a prolonged slump upon his return from a hamstring strain.
But after being bandied around in potential trade discussions last offseason, it’s possible his future with the club could be in question again this winter.
Kyle Tucker: D
The only thing saving this from being an F is the way Tucker finished his otherwise dismal debut season, highlighted by a team-best .333 batting average in the playoffs. Still, the 29-year-old played nowhere near expectations after his $240 offseason signing, setting career-lows in average (.233), OPS (.715) and home runs (17).
The Dodgers will be desperate for him to return to form next year, when he will play an even more vital role in their still-aging lineup. If not, those $60 million player options in 2028 and 2029 will start to feel like poison pills.
Will Smith: C
This is a relatively incomplete grade, given Smith was limited to just 73 games by a three-month neck injury. But even when he did play, the veteran backstop took a step back. His .260 average and .781 OPS were the second-lowest marks of his career (ahead of only 2024). He went just 3-for-31 in the playoffs, salvaging only so much with his Game 3 double in the NLCS.
Tommy Edman: C
After missing the start of the year recovering from ankle surgery, Edman did little more than meet expectations in his utility role with the Dodgers. He was a streaky .247 hitter, finishing with a just-about-league-average .714 OPS. He played good defense and shifted around the diamond. But any more profound impact was limited.
Kiké Hernández: C
Injuries derailed Hernández’s year. And though he had another big October moment –– hitting a home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS –– there was little else to take from his 13th big-league campaign. Once again a free agent, he will represent one of the more intriguing questions of the Dodgers’ winter.
Each of the last three offseasons, they have re-signed him to a one-year deal. Whether they do so again could be a signal for how much, or little, of a shake-up they’re planning for next year.
Dalton Rushing: B
For Rushing, it was a year of promising highs (seven home runs in March/April, .288 batting average in July) and frustrating lows (emotional outbursts early in the year, his spat with Ohtani on the mound in June, and a late-season elbow injury that sidelined him for the playoffs) for the former top prospect. He has more to prove entering Year 3 in 2027.
Alex Freeland: C
Another ex-prospect, Freeland didn’t capitalize on increased opportunity this year, hitting just .234 with only 13 extra-base hits in 89 games. Though still only 25, he remains on the fringes of the team’s long-term plans.
Alex Call: C
The backup outfielder survived the trade deadline. But after hitting just .233 in his reserve role, he might not be a lock to return in his reserve role next year.
Josue De Paula: B+
In his brief MLB debut, De Paula did everything right as a hitter, reaching base at a .500 clip in 11 regular-season games before drawing two key walks as a pinch-hitter in October. Offensively, he seems ready for everyday big-league duties. But the gigantic question mark about his outfield defense leaves his 2027 role unclear entering the winter.
Hyeseong Kim: D
Time will tell if the Dodgers still see something in Kim. But the way he was buried in triple-A this year, after playing just 43 games in the majors in April and May, was not a good sign as he enters the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Hunter Feduccia: B
The former Dodgers farmhand returned to the club in a deadline day trade and was perfectly adequate as the backup catcher over the final couple months of the season. Whether there’s a role for him in the organization again next year remains to be seen.
Miguel Rojas: A
We’re grading on a curve here, in what was a fittingly effective send-off season for the now-retired veteran infielder. Rojas did his job by menacing left-handed pitching (.293 average against them), playing stout defense and serving as a vocal leader in the Dodgers’ star-studded clubhouse. After an accomplished 13-year MLB career –– highlighted by his season-saving home run in Game 7 of last year’s World Series –– his presence will be missed in the clubhouse.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Dodgers' Miguel Rojas, who stole World Series away from Blue Jays, retires
item.dc:creator: Edward Eng
item.description: With one swing of the bat in the ninth inning of Game 7, Miguel Rojas cemented himself in LA Dodgers history. item.content:encoded:
With one swing of the bat in the ninth inning of Game 7, Miguel Rojas cemented himself in LA Dodgers history. Rojas took a pitch from Toronto Blue Jays closer Jeff Hoffman over the fence in left field to tie the series finale at 4-4. It sent shockwaves around Rogers Centre and Blue Jays fans everywhere felt the championship starting to slip away.
After that blast he would further draw the ire of Blue Jays fans when his throw cut down Isiah Kiner-Falefa at the plate in the bottom of the ninth, which prevented him from scoring the winning run. You know the rest of the story. The Dodgers won in extra innings, their second straight title, while Toronto havent' won it all in over three decades.
Rojas played hero for the Dodgers that night and after LA was eliminated from this year's NLCS, Rojas has officially called it a career. Rojas announced the previous year that he intended to retire following the 2026 campaign and he was certainly true to his word.
Miguel Rojas retires from professional baseball with two World Series rings in his collection
That concludes a 13-year major league career that saw him play for only two teams in the big leagues with the Dodgers and Miami Marlins. He began his pro-ball career with the Cincinnati Reds signing as an amateur free agent out of Venezuela in 2006.
In 2012 the Dodgers signed him to a minor league contract and he made his MLB debut in June of 2014. He was then part of a trade that winter that sent 2B Dee Gordon and RHP Dan Haren to the Marlins in exchange for LHP Andrew Heaney, RHP Chris Hatcher, 2B Enrique Hernandez and C Austin Barnes.
He spent the next eight seasons with the Marlins before he was traded back to LA in exchange for SS Jacob Amaya.
Over his career, Rojas compiled a .260 batting average, .677 OPS, along with 457 runs scored, 210 doubles, 11 triples, 61 home runs, 386 RBIs and 68 stolen bases in 1401 career MLB games played. This year in his final season of his baseball career, he posted a .267/.312/.391/.703 slash line, together with 23 runs scored, 16 doubles, four home runs and 23 RBIs in 105 games with Los Angeles.
Rojas may not have collected any personal hardware during his time in the leagues, but he certainly played a role in the Dodgers’ back-to-back World Series wins in 2024 and 2025. He also only hit 61 total dingers for his career, but none was bigger than the lone home run in the ninth on the night of Nov. 1, 2025. That moment alone solidifies him in LA Dodgers lore.

item.title: [rafu.com] 'We Just Got Beat:' Roberts, Ohtani Give Credit to Brewers After NLCS Sweep - Rafu Shimpo
item.dc:creator: Michael Culross

The ball hadn’t yet landed in the right-field pavilion, but the Dodgers and their fans were in full-tilt celebration. Not just because their superstar had hit a home run, but it was a sign that the team’s offensive malaise might finally be breaking, that for the first time in the series, the ball would be bouncin
item.content:encoded:
By MIKEY HIRANO CULROSS
Rafu Sports Editor
Shohei Ohtani flung his bat into the air, exulted toward the sky, and for one shining moment, the improbable seemed more than merely possible.
The ball hadn’t yet landed in the right-field pavilion, but the Dodgers and their fans were in full-tilt celebration. Not just because their superstar had hit a home run, but it was a sign that the team’s offensive malaise might finally be breaking, that for the first time in the series, the ball would be bouncing their way.
The notion of a three-peat for the back-to-back world champs was still alive, regardless of the long odds. At this moment, the team many expected to return to the World Series – and win it – appeared to be returning to form.
The joy was a distant memory by the time Kiké Hernandez’ fly ball settled into left-fielder Jackson Chourio’s glove for the final out of the ninth inning on Thursday, as the Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series and booked their first trip to the World Series since 1982.
In perhaps returning the favor from last year, when the Dodgers won four straight against the Brewers, Milwaukee was the better team in essentially every aspect of the game: starting pitching, relief pitching, batting, situational hitting … they simply played winning baseball.
“They played flawless. They really did,” Dodger manager Dave Roberts said in the postgame press conference, after the visiting Brewers overcame a 4-0 deficit and scored six unanswered runs to complete the sweep.
“I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better,” Roberts said after addressing his team following the loss. “I had a good conversation with the guys in there, and just told them how proud I was. I’m not used to those speeches, those consolation speeches.”
The Brewers had the best record in the major leagues this season, winning 103 games, while L.A. was runner-up with 100 victories.
“For us, it was just pitting two really good ball clubs against one another, and they won out,” Roberts added.
Ohtani’s three-run shot in the second inning was the sole home run of the series for the Dodgers, who had relied heavily on the long ball for wins late in the regular season and into the playoffs.
“I’m very disappointed, but the Brewers are a very good team; you have to give them credit,” Ohtani said through an interpreter in the home clubhouse. “They were able to expose some of our weaknesses.”
For Ohtani, the weaknesses weren’t just stats on a page. He’s been dealing with power-sapping infirmities for months, including a sore right shoulder and gimpy left knee. His last home run came nearly two months prior to Thursday’s shot, and the team shut down his pitching game at the end of July.
He said he is completely committed to returning as a two-way player in 2027, using the off-season to focus on rest, rehab and recovery.
In this year’s NLCS, Ohtani finished batting a paltry .192 with only one home run and 10 strikeouts in 26 at-bats. He had struggled atthe plate to the point there was talk of the unthinkable – Roberts not him starting in Game 4.
After some serious conversation, the manager went with his superstar in the lineup, and early on, at least, it paid off.
“I’ll always trust Shohei. I think he’s the best player on the planet, and he’s not completely healthy,” Roberts explained. “I just give him a lot of respect for not running from it, still wanting to participate, still wanting to play when he’s not 100 percent.”
Roberts noted the rare display of emotion from the Japanese star once the Game 4 home run ball left his bat.
“It was something that you don’t see very often from Shohei. I think it was a lot of pent-up anger, frustration. It was the best ball he hit in probably two, three months, and it was a big hit.
“So I think that for him to look at the dugout, show that emotion, it just shows how much he cares. He’s still human. He still cares and wants to help his team win a baseball game. That was a big hit.”
As gracious as Roberts, Ohtani and the rest of the Dodgers were in defeat, the sting was clear in their voices.
“I’m tremendously grateful for the time we have spent as a team, even though we fell short this year,” Ohtani said. “I want to use this feeling as a catalyst for next season.”
Max Muncy, whose frustrations were laid bare in Game 4 after he struck out with a tying run at third base and slammed his bat to the ground, said he and the Dodgers gave it their best.
“We left it all out there, but the train finally ran out of steam,” Muncy conceded.
The Dodgers were vying to become the first National League team to win three straight World Series titles. The New York Yankees achieved from 1998 to 2000, following the Oakland A’s from 1972 to 1974.
“I certainly think that I wish it was us going to the World Series and defending our crown, but those guys, they earned it, and it’s going to be a heck of a World Series,” Roberts said.
Heading into Game 3 in the American League Championship Series, the Cleveland Guardians held a 2-1 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays. The game scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Saturday due to weather.
The Brewers and Rays are among the five MLB teams that have never won a World Series, along with the San Diego Padres, Seattle Mariners and Colorado Rockies.

item.title: [dailybulletin.com] Analysis: Dodgers’ NLCS defeat raises questions about team’s aging core
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The past two years, the Dodgers’ season ended with parades and calls to “Run it back” for the next season. After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years? “That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning p
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The past two years, the Dodgers’ season ended with parades and calls to “Run it back” for the next season.
After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years?
“That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning player on the Dodgers’ roster (infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement and relief pitcher Blake Treinen, who suffered a shoulder injury late in the season, is a free agent).
“We’ve got a great group of guys. We’ve accomplished a lot of things. We came up short in these four days. But we’ll see where the wind blows this offseason, what happens, what it looks like, what baseball looks like.”
The winds of change could be coming. As Freeman alluded to, the anticipated showdown between MLB’s owners and the players’ union over the next Collective Bargaining Agreement could force the biggest changes in the Dodgers’ future. If the owners are able to get the salary cap or other payroll restrictions they are aiming for, the Dodgers might be forced to change their roster by shedding payroll.
Also looming over the team’s future are the ongoing legal and financial difficulties surrounding principal owner Mark Walter that threaten to eat into the Dodgers’ enormous financial advantages.
Threatening the franchise’s plans to keep its “Golden Era” going more directly, though, is the aging roster. The Brewers certainly made the Dodgers look old in the four-game NLCS sweep.
“I don’t know what you can really say to that. That’s just people’s opinions of what that is,” Freeman said before Game 4. “We do know we have an older team. That doesn’t mean we’re old and we’re playing bad because we’re old. We’re just not playing that great, in my mind.
“But that’s people’s opinions. I can’t change your opinion because we are, in this game, a little bit older than everybody else. I don’t feel old.”
Nonetheless, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman acknowledged awareness – if not overt concern – about the aging core on the team’s roster.
“Yeah, we’ve talked about this a lot,” Friedman said before the start of the NLCS. “With where we are in the success cycle, the success we have had, we have done the opposite of being flippant about it. ‘Oh, it’s great that we won. Now we can put our feet up.’ For us, it’s about pressing the advantage we have right now.
“We have a very talented core, and while a good number of them are getting up there in years, the experience, the way they prepare, the way they play the game, we feel like is a real competitive advantage. So we’ve been aggressive to supplement around that group, all the while pouring ourselves into our next wave.”
The Dodgers’ farm system is indeed as strong as any in MLB. They subtracted two Top 100 prospects (outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-hander River Ryan) in order to trade for pitcher Tarik Skubal in August and still have five more led by outfielder Josue De Paula.
De Paula made the jump from Double-A to the majors in September and showed his readiness in that brief audition. The Dodgers will have to make room for him in their 2027 plan.
That won’t be easy and it’s difficult to see how the Dodgers can get younger in 2027 other than around the margins where Kiké Hernandez acknowledged Game 4 of the NLCS might be his last with the Dodgers and Rojas made it clear, talking to the team after the game and saying he was retiring. He is expected to stay with the organization in some capacity, likely in player development.
“This is it as a player. That was my last game playing. That was the last time I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player,” Rojas said, still in full uniform long after the game ended Thursday night. “From now on, I’m going to start thinking about what’s going to happen in my life as a baseball person other than being a player. I want to start my career on the other side of this business, and I’m looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers as well.
“I’m ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career.”
Hernandez isn’t ready to stop playing. But he knows it might not be in Los Angeles next year.
“I mean, I love this place. I’ve played for three other teams, but every time I look at my career I kind of obviously go back to this place,” the 35-year-old Hernandez said. “I feel like I have a lot left. … I would love to be back. I would love to have one more try, trying to win another one. But I don’t really know what’s going to happen. I hope I’m back, and if I’m not I hope that I get to play for a winning team.”
Seven other Dodgers will become free agents this winter, most prominently bullpen stalwarts Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips and Skubal. Four others – Freeman, outfielder Teoscar Hernandez, third baseman Max Muncy and utility player Hyeseong Kim – are entering the final year of their contracts in 2027, though all but Freeman have club options for 2028.
If the Dodgers are going to change things by their own hand (as opposed to CBA mandate), Teoscar Hernandez clearly has a target on his back as the most likely Dodger to be traded this winter, clearing left field for De Paula. But the Dodgers have largely painted themselves into a corner with this roster. Freeman, shortstop Mookie Betts, catcher Will Smith, center fielder Andy Pages, right fielder Kyle Tucker, two-way star Shohei Ohtani and Muncy, each a year older, are all likely to be in the starting lineup on Opening Day 2027 – whenever that might be.
“I have no idea,” Muncy said of the potential for changes before next season. “That’s for people above me to make those decisions and it’s for me to show up next year, ready to go with whatever group we’ve got. There will come a time when we think about next year. But that’s not at this moment.”
Showing up at Camelback Ranch next spring with the same core is not necessarily a bad thing. Even with only minimal changes, the Dodgers will enter 2027 as the favorites in the National League West once again and a 15th consecutive postseason berth would bring another chance to win the “crapshoot” October has become.
But it also brings this Dodger core closer to “the cliff” Friedman has talked about avoiding.
“It’s tricky because you have to find the right balance,” he said. “It’s hard to transition young players onto your roster. It’s a hard adjustment from Triple-A to the major-league level. We’ve done it some over the years. Some guys we haven’t had the patience long enough to kind of see it through (perhaps an allusion to infielder Miguel Vargas, now an All-Star for the Chicago White Sox).
“That’s the challenge we have with the expectations we have. So we have to be mindful of having a really high standard but also transitioning some of our young players. We’ve seen it some, Andy Pages is featured prominently for us, Will Smith, Alex Freeland got a lot of opportunities this year. Dalton Rushing was a big part when Will missed time. And then late in the year we saw with Josue De Paula.
“We’ve got a lot of guys coming after that as well. So for us it’s about almost having a split personality – to do everything we can to maximize our chances of winning with our major-league roster, and the other side of our personality is pouring ourselves into doing everything we can to have as much talent coming, and we feel really good about that part as well.”

item.title: [aol.com] Shohei Ohtani's health and a possible lockout loom over an uncertain offseason for the Dodgers - AOL
item.dc:creator: BETH HARRIS
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year. Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break. Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss t
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.
___

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] As Dodgers grapple with the end of a dynasty, questions abound for Shohei Ohtani, free agency and the coming labor fight
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock. The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock.
The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure.
Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush that comes with the humbling unmooring of a premature postseason exit. Hugs, daps, thank yous, low-volume answers, goodbyes, regrets. But here it was, here the Dodgers were, in the tricked-out home clubhouse grappling with the end of something.
On one side of the room, Shohei Ohtani stood in front of his locker before a massive semicircle of reporters and TV cameras. For the first time in his MLB career, he'd lost a postseason series. His signing with L.A. ahead of the 2024 season sparked this era of supercharged dominance. And for eight October series his Dodgers were untouchable. Usually, during this spot in the calendar, Ohtani is getting drenched in imitation champagne as Latin rap and joyous roars echo in the background.
The scene Thursday night was a drier, quieter experience.
Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season
This seemingly indomitable baseball behemoth donned street clothes and a New Balance backward cap, small beads of sweat still pooling on his face, trying to explain what went wrong and where he goes from here.
"I haven't been able to really come to grips in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said via interpreter Will Ireton. "I'm going to go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program and see what I can come up with next season."
The postmortem on Los Angeles' crash-out can be as extensive as you choose to make it. But simply put, they were the inferior team. Slower, older, colder and less fearsome than the hard-charging Brewers. Baseball's most aged offense failed to slug and didn't perform with runners in scoring position. One of the most talented rotations ever assembled wasn't dominant enough to make up the difference.
All season, the Dodgers touted their experience as a calling card. Perhaps, if the series had been closer, that might have mattered. As it stands, it's less necessary to assign blame when so much went wrong.
"I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better," manager Dave Roberts said after his team's 6-4 loss in Game 4.
The morning after, fans across the baseball universe are celebrating the Dodgers' downfall. They aren't the only ones. As Milwaukee's champagne celebration roared in the visiting clubhouse, Brewers coaches and executives were already receiving texts of appreciation and congratulations on slaying the mighty dragon.
But don't expect the upcoming small-market Fall Classic to remedy baseball's impending labor struggle. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, the league and the owners have been pushing hard for the adoption of a salary cap. Certainly, that argument becomes at least somewhat trickier to make with the half-billion-dollar boogeyman Dodgers on vacation, but the league won't suddenly change course after four games. The showdown over a cap was always going to be drawn-out and messy, no matter which team is the last one standing.
For the Dodgers organization, the uncertainty about baseball's future further complicates what was always going to be a critical offseason. One October exit won't kill off this juggernaut. Neither will a new economic landscape. The Dodgers remain advantageously positioned to compete for championships over the next decade and beyond. That's a testament to both their player-development prowess and their imposing spending power.
But the questions are already piling on Andrew Friedman's desk. Surely, the president of baseball operations is already considering the future and how this winter will shape the 2027 Dodgers.
No task is more important than figuring out what went wrong with Ohtani's season. For three months, the two-way star was, for the first time as a Dodger, doing full two-way stardom. Another MVP felt like an inevitability. Then his biceps started barking. A start on the mound was pushed back, then scratched, then so was another. Ohtani didn't throw a single in-game pitch after July 3.
His attempts to get back on the mound then appeared to compromise his offensive talents. He got ice-cold in late August into September. His physicality began to fray. His body wasn't right. Eventually, the Dodgers had no choice but to place him on the injured list. Only over the last two days of the Dodgers' postseason did Ohtani look anything like himself.
Communication with the four-time MVP has rarely been perfect. Some of that is the language barrier. Some of that is Ohtani's lone ranger approach. But now both sides need to evaluate why a diminished version of Ohtani was forced to play through pain. After the Game 4 loss, Ohtani told reporters that he intends to pitch next season. In what capacity remains to be seen. It might behoove the Dodgers to slow-play his recovery timeline to ensure he's available when they need him most — in the postseason.
There are a mountain of transactional questions as well. Tarik Skubal, added in a deadline blockbuster, is now a free agent. Will the Dodgers flex their muscles to re-sign him? Or do they want to give younger arms such as Roki Sasaki, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski some rotation runway? What about upper-level pitching prospects such as Christian Zazueta, Zach Root, Adam Serwinowski and Jackson Ferris? Could they let Skubal walk in favor of a different free-agent starter? Freddy Peralta has looked pretty good recently.
Positionally, though, is where Los Angeles' bigger roster-construction conversations will take place. They got mollywhopped by Milwaukee in part because the Dodgers' offense looked unathletic and elderly. Friedman has expressed a desire to inject more youth into the group, but that's easier said than done. A number of spots feel set in stone: Ohtani at DH, Will Smith at catcher, Freddie Freeman at first, Mookie Betts at short, Kyle Tucker in right field, Andy Pages in center.
Max Muncy (3B) and Teoscar Hernández (LF) are older players expected to reach free agency after 2027. A trade of either could be a way to reshuffle the deck, with Hernández the likelier to go. Tommy Edman had a second straight mediocre, injury-marred campaign, but he has four seasons left on his contract. Might the Dodgers seek a suitor for the switch-hitting utilityman?
Even after harvesting the farm for the Skubal trade, Los Angeles has one of the most stocked systems in the sport. Most of their prospect juice is concentrated in the outfield. Five Dodgers outfield prospects at Double-A or above — Josue De Paula, Eduardo Quintero, Mike Sirota, Charles Davalan and James Tibbs III — could find themselves on offseason top-100 lists. De Paula, who impressed in a late-season cup of coffee, Quintero and Sirota are currently ranked fourth, 15th and 17th, respectively, by MLB Pipeline.
Unfortunately for the Dodgers, you can play only three outfielders at a time. In their existing outfield, they already have the highest-paid player in the sport (Tucker) and the starting center fielder in the 2026 All-Star Game (Pages). With just one spot remaining, it'll be fascinating to see how Friedman makes use of his farm system.
For the players, none of these contingencies or scenarios will offer any short-term solace. They aimed for a three-peat and missed. That sting will take time to subside, even if the 2027 Dodgers project to be a similarly formidable force.
"We fell short, you know?" utilityman Kiké Hernández lamented postgame. "We had a good run, but here we are."

item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee Brewers World Series Outlook After the Sweep
PUERTO RICO · WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
The Milwaukee Brewers World Series outlook is bright, with the best 2026 record in baseball and a 7-1 run through the playoffs. The Brewers swept the Dodgers 4-0 in the National League series that ended on Thursday 15 October.
The final opens in Milwaukee on Friday 23 October against Cleveland or Tampa Bay, whichever wins the American League series. Puerto Rico, a US territory, has no Puerto Rico-born player among those the three clubs left have used in the playoffs, MLB box scores show.
The Milwaukee Brewers World Series Outlook in Numbers
Milwaukee won 103 games and lost 59 in the regular season, the best record in baseball, MLB standings show. The Dodgers followed at 100-62, Tampa Bay at 98-64 and Cleveland at 85-77.
In the division series, Milwaukee beat San Diego 3-1, winning Games 1, 2 and 4 by one or two runs. The Padres took Game 3 by 4-3 on Tuesday 6 October.
Against Los Angeles the Brewers won 2-1, 7-4, 6-2 and 6-4, outscoring the Dodgers 21-11 over the four games. Game 4 began with the Dodgers ahead 4-0 after two innings, and Milwaukee then scored six runs without reply.
Milwaukee is 7-1 in the postseason so far. It now has seven days without a game before Game 1 on Friday 23 October.
Who Milwaukee Could Face in the Final
Cleveland leads Tampa Bay 2-1 in the American League Championship Series after a 3-2 win in Game 3 on Thursday 15 October. Tampa Bay, which won 98 games to Cleveland’s 85, took Game 2 by 3-1 after losing Game 1 by 7-3.
Game 4 is on Friday 16 October and Game 5 on Saturday 17 October, both at Progressive Field in Cleveland. Games 6 and 7, if needed, are at Tropicana Field on Monday 19 and Tuesday 20 October.
The opponent is therefore known by Tuesday 20 October at the latest, and the World Series dates do not change. A Cleveland win in Game 4 would leave it one win from the final.
MLB box scores show 17 Latin American-born players used by the three clubs in the playoffs so far: six in Milwaukee, five in Cleveland, six in Tampa Bay. Milwaukee has four Venezuelans, including Jackson Chourio and William Contreras, and two Dominicans.
Cleveland lists three Dominicans, among them José Ramírez, plus one Venezuelan and one Panamanian. Tampa Bay lists three Dominicans, two Cubans, among them Yandy Díaz, and one Mexican.
The World Series Schedule
Games 1 and 2 are at American Family Field in Milwaukee on Friday 23 October and Saturday 24 October. MLB lists Games 3, 4 and 5 for Monday 26, Tuesday 27 and Wednesday 28 October, with the venue still to be decided.
Games 6 and 7 return to Milwaukee on Friday 30 and Saturday 31 October, if the series is still open. First-pitch times were not final in the MLB data reviewed.
For the Puerto Rican players behind the sweep, read Puerto Rico Dodgers Milwaukee Baseball Connection Explained. For the wider island picture, see Puerto Rico in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances.
Daily results across the region are in Latin America Sports Daily for Friday, October 16, 2026. It follows the playoffs alongside other Latin American sport.
What Prediction Markets Say
Polymarket’s World Series winner market gave Milwaukee a 65.4% chance at 1:37 p.m. ET on Friday 16 October, with Cleveland at 19.4% and Tampa Bay at 15.2%. A price of 65 cents reads as a 65% chance, and these are bets, not polls.
The market has traded about US$45.1 million in total, including about US$2.0 million on the Brewers contract. Over the previous day Milwaukee gained about 9.0 points and Cleveland about 4.2, while Tampa Bay lost about 5.8 after Thursday’s games.
Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.
What It Means for You
For US readers, the final opens in Wisconsin on Friday 23 October, with Milwaukee at home for the first two games. Ticket and broadcast details were not reviewed, so check MLB’s official channels.
For Puerto Rican fans, MLB box scores show no Puerto Rico-born player used by the Brewers, Guardians or Rays in the playoffs through Thursday 15 October. The Latin American presence is Venezuelan, Dominican, Cuban, Panamanian and Mexican instead.
What Is Not Known
Milwaukee’s opponent is not known, because Cleveland led Tampa Bay 2-1 and Game 4 was still to be played. The result settles it by Tuesday 20 October at the latest.
Rosters can still change before Game 1, so the player counts shown here are as of Friday 16 October. The MLB data reviewed give no starting pitchers or first-pitch times for the final.
Nothing reviewed measures how many Puerto Ricans will watch or which team they will back. Market prices are a snapshot of bets on Friday 16 October and not a forecast.
Frequently Asked Questions
When does the 2026 World Series start?
Game 1 is on Friday 23 October at American Family Field in Milwaukee. Game 2 follows there on Saturday 24 October.
Who will Milwaukee play in the World Series?
That depends on the American League series between Cleveland and Tampa Bay, which Cleveland led 2-1 on Friday 16 October. The opponent is known by Tuesday 20 October at the latest.
What was Milwaukee’s record in 2026?
Milwaukee finished 103-59, the best record in Major League Baseball. It is 7-1 in the postseason after beating San Diego 3-1 and Los Angeles 4-0.
What do prediction markets say about the final?
Polymarket gave Milwaukee about 65% on 16 October, 1:37 p.m. ET, with Cleveland near 19% and Tampa Bay near 15%. Those prices are bets, not polls, and they move within minutes.
Are any Puerto Rican players left in the playoffs?
MLB box scores through 15 October show none on the Brewers, Guardians or Rays. Edwin Díaz and Enrique Hernández left with the Dodgers.

item.title: [finchannel] Miguel Rojas retires after Dodgers’ NLCS exit, with plans to remain in baseball - FINCHANNEL

item.content:encoded:
Miguel Rojas retired Thursday, October 15, at 37 after the Los Angeles Dodgers’ elimination from the National League Championship Series. The infielder’s final game ended with Milwaukee completing a four-game sweep, leaving him to discuss a planned move into another role with the organization where he began his major league career.
Speaking to reporters at Dodger Stadium, Rojas confirmed that his playing career was over. True Blue LA reported that he wanted to stay with the Dodgers, with an anticipated emphasis on player development, although the precise role remained undetermined. His retirement was also reported by MLB.com, the Los Angeles Times and Fox’s OutKick.
Rojas finished after 13 major league seasons split between Los Angeles and the Miami Marlins. His second Dodgers stint included two World Series championships and the home run that tied Game 7 of the 2025 championship against Toronto. He returned for one final season in 2026 after signing a one-year, $5.5 million contract.
A final game without a plate appearance
Rojas played two innings at second base in Thursday’s finale but did not bat, according to True Blue LA’s account. His final two major league plate appearances had come in Game 3 on Wednesday, when he singled and walked. All seven of his plate appearances in this postseason came against left-handed pitching.
The account listed a double alongside that single and walk in his final postseason. During the 2026 regular season, he hit .293 against left-handers, with a .340 on-base percentage and .469 slugging percentage. Those figures describe his production against left-handed pitchers, rather than his overall season.
MLB’s regular-season figures show that Rojas hit .267 with four home runs and 23 runs batted in during 2026.
The Dodgers’ season ended in a 6-4 loss after they had built a four-run lead. Shohei Ohtani supplied a three-run homer in the second inning off Dustin May. Milwaukee erased the advantage by the fifth, then moved ahead on Garrett Mitchell’s sixth-inning home run against Tanner Scott.
David Hamilton added a ninth-inning solo homer. Aaron Ashby completed a three-inning save, closing a game in which Los Angeles had doubles in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings without scoring those runners. The Dodgers went 2 for 11 with runners in scoring position Thursday.
The Brewers advanced to their first World Series since 1982 and their first as a National League club. For Los Angeles, the defeat ended the pursuit of a third consecutive championship. Rojas addressed his teammates after manager Dave Roberts’s postgame meeting, according to MLB.com’s account of the clubhouse.
Returning for the last season
The decision followed a plan Rojas had discussed before the 2026 season. MLB.com’s December 2025 report on his new contract said he intended the coming year to be his last. The deal kept him in Los Angeles after an October in which he had rarely started before the final two World Series games.
True Blue LA’s report on that contract described a 2025 regular season in which he batted .262 with a .318 on-base percentage and .397 slugging percentage. He started more often at second and third base than at shortstop, the position he had played regularly earlier in his career.
His October assignment changed in Toronto. Rojas started at second base in Games 6 and 7 after starting only twice in the Dodgers’ first 15 postseason games. In Game 6, he handled the throw from left fielder Kiké Hernández to complete the double play that ended the game.
In Game 7, his solo homer with one out in the ninth tied the score. He also fielded a grounder in the bottom of that inning and threw home to prevent Toronto from scoring the winning run. The Dodgers subsequently won in extra innings.
A return trade and a changing infield role
Rojas made his Dodgers debut in 2014 before being traded to Miami that December in the larger deal involving Dee Gordon. He spent eight seasons with the Marlins, then returned to Los Angeles in January 2023 in exchange for shortstop Jake Amaya.
In eight of his first nine major league seasons, Rojas played for manager Don Mattingly. That stretch included his 2014 Dodgers debut and years in Miami, where he established himself as a regular shortstop.
The January 2023 account of the trade described a player whose defensive record offered Los Angeles experienced depth. Rojas had batted .236 in 2022, with a .283 on-base percentage and .323 slugging percentage. That season he tied Houston’s Jeremy Peña for the most Defensive Runs Saved among major league shortstops, with 15, according to the report.
He had been a National League Gold Glove finalist at shortstop in both 2020 and 2022. The Dodgers acquired him as Gavin Lux was preparing to take on a larger role at the position. Rojas also brought experience at third base and second base, giving the team alternatives across the infield.
Lux’s spring-training knee injury subsequently changed the arrangement. In a May 2024 report, True Blue LA recalled that Rojas had started 109 games during the previous season. In spring 2024, Mookie Betts was moving into an everyday shortstop role, with Rojas among those helping him make the transition.
Mentorship alongside the playing time
Roberts publicly credited Rojas, along with coaches Dino Ebel and Chris Woodward, for the work Betts had put into shortstop in 2024. The veteran’s assistance also included pregame drills and conversations during games, according to Eric Stephen’s reporting for True Blue LA.
That report described Rojas helping Lux return to second base and working with Miguel Vargas when Vargas was learning the position in 2023. Rojas invited Vargas to work out with him in Florida after being acquired by the Dodgers. He told the outlet that coaching was part of his ambition after his playing days.
In that 2024 interview, Rojas recalled Adrián González helping him as a rookie, including conversations about baseball and professional life off the field.
Three consecutive clubhouse awards
The recognition from teammates and coaches continued in September, when Rojas was voted the Dodgers’ Roy Campanella Award winner for 2026. The award honors the player judged to embody the Hall of Fame catcher’s leadership and spirit. Rojas had also won in 2024 and 2025.
According to the September account of the award, he became the first Dodger to receive it in three consecutive seasons. Justin Turner was the only other three-time recipient, with wins in 2017, 2019 and 2020.
Clayton Kershaw and Chase Utley had each won twice. Kershaw received the honor in 2013 and 2014, and Utley in 2016 and 2018.
The same report noted that Rojas had started games at second base, shortstop and third base during 2026 and had also played three innings at first. It described his plans to join the organization’s front office with a focus on developing players. Thursday’s retirement account left the precise assignment open.
Questions and answers
Did Rojas play for teams other than the Dodgers?
Yes. He spent eight major league seasons with Miami between his two periods in Los Angeles.
Was retirement already part of his plan?
He had said before the 2026 season that it would be his last as a player.
Will he stay with the Dodgers?
Rojas said he wanted to remain with the organization. Reporting described a prospective player-development role, with its precise form still undetermined.
