item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

item.content:encoded:
Los Cerveceros de Milwaukee clavaron este jueves el último clavo en el ataúd de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, al imponerse en el cuarto desafío de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional para sellar una sensacional e inesperada barrida.
De esta forma, dejaron vacante el trono de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) y, con ello, impidieron al conjunto californiano —y, dentro del mismo, al cubano Andy Pagés— alcanzar su tercer anillo consecutivo de campeón.
El desenlace del pulso, sellado con una pizarra de 6-4 en la casa de los monarcas de las dos más recientes ediciones de la Serie Mundial, ya es una gran hazaña para un equipo que llevaba 44 años sin acceder a la disputa por el trofeo mayor.
THE NATIONAL LEAGUE PENNANT IS COMING HOME TO MILWAUKEE
#WinOurWay https://t.co/AC1ckMgXxM
— Milwaukee Brewers (@Brewers) October 16, 2026
Impulso insuficiente
Aferrados a la épica, los Dodgers salieron dispuestos a evitar el escarnio, y en la segunda entrada un imparable de Pagés puso a funcionar la pizarra.
A continuación, el japonés Shohei Ohtani rompió una sequía de casi dos meses sin conectar jonrones con un batazo de tres carreras, y dar una ventaja de 4-0 a los locales, que parecían encaminados a extender la batalla a un quinto partido.
Sin embargo, como sucedió en los pulsos previos, Milwaukee aguardó el mejor momento para otro ataque demoledor.
En la cuarta entrada, el venezolano William Contreras conectó el primer imparable de los visitantes con un doble de regla, y Jake Bauers siguió con un batazo similar para descontar. Los visitantes consiguieron equilibrar el marcador paso a paso mediante paciencia, astucia en las bases y un colapso del bullpen de los rivales.
La remontada se completó en el sexto inning, cuando Garrett Mitchell conectó un jonrón solitario y en el noveno episodio David Hamilton selló el triunfo con otro vuelacercas sin compañeros en circulación.
GARRETT MITCHELL WILL NOT BE DENIED https://t.co/pTKyUKW7kM
— Milwaukee Brewers (@Brewers) October 16, 2026
Pagés no alcanza
En medio de la debacle, Pagés emergió como el bateador más oportuno de los Dodgers en la serie y los números lo demuestran: el equipo tenía cuatro imparables en 34 turnos con corredores en posición anotadora y tres llevaron la impronta del pinareño.
Además de firmar el remolque de la primera anotación, el cubano lideró los últimos intentos de por cambiar la historia.
En el séptimo abrió con un doble y avanzó a tercera con el toque de sacrificio de Kike Hernández. Sin embargo, los Cerveceros conjuraron la amenaza con un ponche del zurdo Aaron Ashby a Ohtani y un fallo de Mookie Betts con roletazo al cuadro.
Más allá del resultado, la actuación del vueltabajero queda como una especie de redención, teniendo en cuenta su aporte el pasado año.
Andy Pages has more hits with RISP this postseason than the entire Dodgers team COMBINED 😳 https://t.co/hdWUrAfqO3
— Just Baseball (@JustBB_Media) October 16, 2026
En octubre de 2025, Pagés bateó de 51-4 (.078) y perdió su puesto de titular en el jardín durante la Serie Mundial ante Toronto. Su OPS de .211 fue el peor de cualquier jugador con al menos 50 apariciones al plato en una sola postemporada.
Los fantasmas de aquellos tiempos le atormentaron en el inicio del tramo decisivo, al conectar solo un hit en los dos primeros desafíos. Sin embargo, todo cambió el 7 de octubre en Atlanta con un sencillo productor de dos carreras en el séptimo inning del Juego 4, que dio a los Dodgers la ventaja definitiva en el 4-1 sobre los Bravos.
Como consuelo le queda la nominación al premio Guante de Oro de la Liga Nacional como defensor de la pradera central.
☑️🇨🇺 Andy Pagés has been named one of three finalists for the National League Gold Glove Award in center field.
👉🏻 The Pinar del Río native joins fellow nominees Pete Crow-Armstrong (Cubs) and Michael Harris II (Braves). Andy played elite defense in 2026, but PCA is the clear favorite to take home the award.
📊 During the regular season, he recorded eight Outs Above Average (OAA), 14 outfield assists and 20 Defensive Runs Saved (DRS).
ℹ️ Pelota Cubana
— Cuban Baseball Digest 🇺🇸🇨🇺 (@CBaseballDigest) October 15, 2026
Cerveceros degustan la venganza
Lo sucedido en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional tiene sabor a desquite. En 2025 fueron los Dodgers quienes barrieron a Milwaukee en cuatro juegos, con Ohtani llevándose la distinción de Jugador Más Valioso (MVP).
Ahora, los de Milwaukee se convirtieron en el primer equipo en barrer al mismo rival que los había barrido en la postemporada anterior.
Además, se erigieron como el quinto equipo en la historia de la MLB en superar un déficit de cuatro o más carreras para cerrar una serie al mejor de siete, y el primero en hacerlo para completar una barrida.
The moment your Milwaukee Brewers raised the Warren C. Giles Trophy
#WinOurWay https://t.co/z7P6bd2XVq
— Milwaukee Brewers (@Brewers) October 16, 2026
Para la franquicia de Milwaukee, resulta uno de los puntos más altos de su historia, solo comparable con la llegada a la única oportunidad anterior en que avanzaron a la Serie Mundial. Sucedió en 1982, cuando el equipo competía en la Liga Americana, y terminaron perdiéndola ante los Cardenales de San Luis.
Para los Dodgers, en cambio, representa un duro golpe en su objetivo de establecer una nueva dinastía en la MLB. Los californianos buscaban convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas, pero terminaron barridos en su propio estadio en la Serie de Campeonato.
Los Cerveceros esperan ahora a su rival de la Serie Mundial, el cual se definirá en el duelo entre los Rays de Tampa Bay —donde militan los cubanos Yandy Díaz y Víctor Mesa Jr.— y los Guardianes de Cleveland. Estos últimos lideran la serie 2-1 tras su victoria de ayer con pizarra de 3-2 y este viernes buscarán ampliar su ventaja jugando nuevamente como locales.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers waste late opportunities as failures in the clutch burn them again in NLCS finale
item.dc:creator: Jeff Fletcher
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With all their financial might, the Dodgers couldn’t buy a hit when they needed it most. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With all their financial might, the Dodgers couldn’t buy a hit when they needed it most.
The Dodgers’ bid for a three-peat came to an end, in large part because their star-studded lineup managed just four hits in 27 at-bats with runners in scoring position while losing all four games of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
Was it the excellence of the Brewers’ pitchers or the failure of the Dodgers’ hitters in those moments?
“It’s a little bit of both,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “I think it’s their bullpen being extremely good and making pitches, and then I think it’s us just not getting the job done, but ultimately, that’s why this damn thing is so hard, you know? Just getting to the end is just really, really, really hard. I don’t know if people talk about it enough, but you have to have a lot of things go your way. You have to have a little luck. You have to have skill. You have to have talent. You have to have decisions, and it all has to kind of go your way to get to the end and we just didn’t have it this year.”
There were signs in the second half of the season that the Dodgers weren’t firing on all cylinders, when their offense began to slow down. And even in winning their NL Division Series against the Atlanta Braves, their power covered up the problem.
The Dodgers managed to hit eight homers in that series, accounting for 11 of their 14 runs.
They were 1 for 16 with runners in scoring position. For the postseason, they were 5 for 43.
Two of those hits came in the second inning on Thursday, when Andy Pages punched a run-scoring single up the middle and then Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer.
At that point, the Dodgers had a 4-0 lead and the ballpark was rocking. The party seemed like it was just starting, but it was actually ending.
The Dodgers didn’t get another hit with a runner in scoring position in the game.
“I don’t know,” outfielder Teoscar Hernandez said. “I think better decisions when it comes to swinging the bat. But sometimes you’ve got to give the other side credit, you know? They have one of the best bullpens in the history of baseball. It’s hard when you’re facing a guy that is attacking you with everything that they got and and making pitches, being aggressive and you don’t get the results that you want.”
The final four innings of Game 4 were particularly painful for the Dodgers. Just after the Brewers took a 5-4 lead in the top of the sixth, the Dodgers had a runner in scoring position in three straight innings.
The Dodgers went hitless in six official at-bats with runners in scoring position – plus one sacrifice. In two of those, they had a runner at third with less than two outs.
The frustrating sequence began when Kyle Tucker ripped a one-out double in the sixth, but Hernandez grounded out and Muncy struck out.
In the seventh, Pages led off with a double. After Kiké Hernandez bunted him to third, Ohtani struck out on three pitches and then Mookie Betts grounded out.
With one out in the eighth, Will Smith ripped one down the right field line, for a double, and he took third base as the ball skipped past right fielder Sal Frelick.
Just 90 feet from a tie game, the Dodgers came up empty again. Tucker hit a fly ball to shallow center field and then Hernandez struck out.
The Dodgers went down in order in the ninth, ending their season.
Afterward, first baseman Freddie Freeman was asked how “deflating” it was to continually come up empty in so many opportunities when they just needed a hit.
“Everything’s deflating now,” Freeman said. “I know there wasn’t one pitch, one at-bat. They just outplayed us in the series, which is kind of how it goes. We had our opportunities. We didn’t get the job done.”

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers three-peat bid ends with NLCS sweep by Brewers
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

item.title: [mlb.com] Brewers end Dodgers' three-peat bid with an NLCS sweep of their own
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it. The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end. The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned.
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it.
The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end.
The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned. For the first time in 44 years, the Brewers are heading to the World Series. They beat Los Angeles, 6-4, in Game 4 on Thursday night. Next week, Milwaukee will host the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982.
And could this ending have been any more fitting?
Three times in the last decade, the Brewers had been expelled from the postseason by Los Angeles. A year ago, they were swept away with relative ease, as the Dodgers set a course for their second consecutive World Series title. It went unspoken, but all summer, the Brewers seemed to know: If they were going to get where they wanted to go, this was the team they needed to beat.
Thursday’s clincher did not come easy. Why should it? These Brewers don’t do easy. They fell behind 4-0 in the second inning. Dodger Stadium shook when Shohei Ohtani’s titanic three-run blast landed deep in the right-field pavilion.
But the Brewers did what these Brewers do. They answered. Two runs in the fourth. Two more in the fifth. Garrett Mitchell’s go-ahead home run in the sixth, and David Hamilton’s insurance blast in the ninth. Shortly thereafter, the Brewers were celebrating a first in MLB history: They became the first team to sweep the very same team that had eliminated them via sweep in the previous postseason.
Across four games, every punch the Dodgers threw was returned with a Milwaukee counterpunch. Facing elimination on Thursday, Los Angeles moved Ohtani back into the leadoff spot. He’s the best player on the planet, when healthy, and if the Dodgers were going to go down … why go down with anyone else at the top of their lineup?
That meant it was Ohtani who strode to the plate against Brewers right-handed reliever Dustin May with two on and two out in the second. May threw a 1-1 cutter. It hung. Ohtani unleashed that ferocious left-handed swing with a bit of an uppercut. (You know the one, even if it had been a while since you last saw it.) The ball carried to the very back of the right-field pavilion, Ohtani’s first home run since Aug. 18.
Dodger Stadium erupted. The two-time defending champs had life. They led 4-0 in the second inning. They had Tarik Skubal lined up for Game 5. And Yoshinobu Yamamoto for Game 6. And Blake Snell for Game 7. Maybe, just maybe …
The Brewers had other ideas. William Contreras and Jake Bauers hit back-to-back doubles in the fourth, cutting the Dodgers’ lead to 4-2. An inning later, Sal Frelick walked and stole a base, then scored on Hamilton’s RBI single. Tyler Glasnow’s night was done after 4 1/3 innings. A few batters later, Bauers plated the tying run with a bases-loaded walk.
Mitchell led off the sixth by pulverizing a Tanner Scott fastball, and the Brewers had the lead. They held onto it for dear life. Aaron Ashby stranded the tying run in scoring position in the seventh. Then again in the eighth.
He just kept going. Ashby got Kiké Hernández to line out to Jackson Chourio in left field to end it, and with that, the Brewers had their first National League pennant. (When they last reached the Fall Classic in 1982, they did so in the American League.) In the coming weeks, they’ll get a chance for another first: their first World Series title. Either the Rays or Guardians will stand in their way.
But first, a party 44 years in the making.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year aft
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.
Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
1. The Brewers
Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best team
We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.
"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.
2. Shohei Ohtani
MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.
Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, , and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.
3. Freddie Freeman
Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:
- Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.
- Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.
- Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.
- Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.
That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.
4. The supporting cast
Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCS
Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴
5. Dave Roberts
Roberts did not push the right buttons
The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.
De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers face an offseason reckoning after stunning NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning. Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench. He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more. With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration. His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over. But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run. This was a last stand. The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milw
item.content:encoded:
The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning.
Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench.
He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more.
With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration.
His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over.
But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run.
This was a last stand.
The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milwaukee Brewers saw that it wouldn’t.
As they did throughout this National League Championship Series, the Brewers pressed and pressed and pressed. Little by little, the Dodgers gave in.
By the sixth inning, the Dodgers were behind. Three innings later, they were officially eliminated from the playoffs when Kiké Hernández flied out to left field against Aaron Ashby for the final out of a 6-4 defeat at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers didn’t just lose.
They were swept in four games by the same team they swept at this stage of the postseason last year.
Now, comes the hard part.
The Dodgers might be the second-best team in baseball behind the Brewers, but they can’t return with a similar roster next season and expect the results to be any different.
Farewells are in order.
Farewell to long-time Dodgers who will forever be known in these parts as World Series heroes.
Farewell to Ohtani hitting and pitching full-time.
With how the Dodgers were thumped by the Brewers, president of baseball operation Andrew Friedman has a clear directive.
Adjust – or else.
The Dodgers have the oldest team in the major leagues. First baseman Freddie Freeman and infielder Miguel Rojas are 37. Third baseman Max Muncy is 36 and utilityman Kiké Hernández is 35. Shortstop Mookie Betts and outfielder Teoscar Hernández are 34.
The problem is magnified by their prime-aged players, who are breaking down as if they are senior citizens.
Ohtani, 32, was obviously debilitated in the postseason, which explains why a former 50-homer player wasn’t a power threat for the majority of these playoffs.
Catcher Will Smith, 31, was sidelined for three months with a disc problem, which contributed to him being out of sorts in the batter’s box.
Utilityman Tommy Edman, also 31, is an All-Star-caliber player when healthy – but he often isn’t.
Kyle Tucker, 29, flat-out stunk for the majority of the first season of his four-year, $240-million contract.
What Friedman and others in the front office will have to decide in the coming weeks and months is how quickly and drastically they will turn over the roster.
The Dodgers shopped Teoscar Hernández last offseason, and they figure to do so again this offseason, as they already have a promising in-house replacement for him in left field in 21-year-old rookie Josue De Paula. Hernández has only one more guaranteed year remaining on his contract.
But what do the Dodgers do beyond that?
Do they attempt to move some of their other veterans? Or do they field more or less the same team next season, accept the limitations of their roster, and wait for some of their contracts to expire in another year?
Freeman will be an unrestricted free agent after the 2027 season. Muncy could also depart that winter, as his option for the 2028 season is a team option.
There are no simple answers.
Muncy’s option for 2028 is a relative bargain at $10 million, for example. The Dodgers might not be able to find a better third baseman at that price point.
Or, in the case of Freeman, how can they not re-sign a player as beloved as he is?
One factor that could influence the Dodgers’ team-building approach: Baseball’s next collective-bargaining agreement.
More restrictive spending limits of some kind figure to be on their way, as franchise owners are pushing for a salary cap. The Dodgers could be forced to dump salaries whether they want to or not.
Whatever happens on that front, the Dodgers will have to address Ohtani’s situation.
Ohtani broke into Japan’s top league as an 18 year old. He was a two-way player in the five seasons he played for the Nippon-Ham Fighters, and his body has plenty of mileage on it.
This season was particularly demanding.
Last year, resumed pitching in the middle of the season after recovering from his second major elbow operation. This year, he attempted to be a full-time hitter and pitcher for the entire season.
Ohtani broke down. He abandoned pitching in the middle of the season. The resulting injuries diminished him as a hitter.
Knowing Ohtani will insist on remaining a two-way player, what do the Dodgers do?
Do they spread out his starts to extend the periods between his starts? Or do they try to sell him on the idea that by not pitching in the early parts of the season, he could be a two-way player in October?
The results have spoken.
Changes will have to be made.

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to book ticket to World Series
item.dc:creator: Ben Nicholson-Smith
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it. As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over. There were late chances to score Kyle Tu
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it.
As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over.
There were late chances to score Kyle Tucker from second and Will Smith from third, but in the end the Dodgers failed.
They’re a great team, but not the best team in baseball anymore, or even the best team in the National League. That honour goes to the Milwaukee Brewers, who secured the pennant with a sweep of the Dodgers thanks to Mitchell’s big swing, some tenacious rallies in the middle innings and impressive relief pitching.
The win overshadowed a dramatic home run from Shohei Ohtani and disappointed 49,104 fans still hoping for a third straight championship. Instead, it’s Milwaukee who will represent the National League in the World Series in a battle of small markets against either Cleveland or Tampa Bay.
All series, the Brewers outplayed the Dodgers. They hit more home runs, they played better defence and they pitched better. And really, that should come as no surprise. This team has reached the post-season eight of the last nine seasons, including each of the last four NL Central titles.
But still, the Dodgers are baseball’s preeminent team, so when Shohei Ohtani demolished a Dustin May cutter to give the Dodgers an early 4-0 lead, their path to victory seemed to open up again. As the ball soared into the right-field bleachers, Ohtani bounced backwards towards first base and yelled at his teammates in the third-base dugout. It may be the most emotion he’s ever shown on a big-league field.
Considering the context, Ohtani’s home run was all the more significant. Just two days ago, there was talk of benching him given his middling performance and knee and biceps injuries. Then came a stellar performance in Game 3 and his Game 4 home run, the first one he’s hit since August 18.
But aside from Ohtani’s big swing, the Dodgers simply didn’t have answers offensively. No one else homered in the NLCS. In fact, they had just five other extra-base hits this series — all doubles. A team known for its high-powered offence had produced backup-catcher type numbers when it counted most.
They needed to hit or see their season end, no in-between. And they didn’t hit, so their season ended.
The Brewers, on the other hand, managed just enough offence. David Hamilton added a late home run and breakout star Jake Bauers drove in three, including two with a pivotal double in the fourth inning. All series, they found answers against the Dodgers team that allowed the fewest runs in MLB this regular season.
Oddly enough, this will be the first time the Brewers represent the National League in the World Series. When they made it in 1982, they were still an American League team and lost to the Cardinals in seven games.
The Dodgers were seeking the first MLB three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees and only the fifth in MLB history (Athletics 1972-74; Yankees 1949-53; Yankees 1936-39). Instead, they’ll turn their attention to the off-season, with Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, Alex Vesia and, most notably, Tarik Skubal all headed for free agency.
Before then, the Brewers will participate in a World Series featuring two of MLB’s lowest payrolls, undermining the narrative that MLB needs a salary cap for small-market teams to compete. The Brewers didn’t just beat the Dodgers, they dominated them thanks to elite player acquisition, strong player development and a strong team culture.
Soon enough, more tests await the Brewers. First, though, it’s time for a well deserved celebration.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
item.description: Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4 One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship. Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday night, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk to raise his batting average to .182.
"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at," manager Dave Roberts said before the game. "I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."
(Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Ohtani typically leads off the order but has been dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps for the last few months. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the lineup.
Roberts said Ohtani has given him reasons to believe in the four-time MVP, citing Ohtani staying until 9 p.m. on Tuesday to work on his swing and his improved at-bat quality.
"Baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top," he said. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs."
Roberts tweaked the entire lineup after Wednesday's loss put the Dodgers on the brink of elimination. Mookie Betts, who led off in Game 3, was bumped to No. 2, while Freddie Freeman moved to No. 3.
Will Smith, whose offensive struggles mirrored Ohtani's, moved up to fourth from seventh. Smith doubled in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers briefly took a 2-1 lead.
"I thought Will took very good at-bats, big hit yesterday," Roberts said. "He’s been in big spots."
Kyle Tucker hit fifth, while Teoscar Hernandez went from third to sixth. Miguel Rojas hit seventh and Andy Pages dropped to eighth from fifth.
Kiké Hernández, who came off the bench in Game 3, hit ninth, with regular third baseman Max Muncy available to come off the bench for Rojas or Kiké Hernández.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [MLB.com] Back to basics: Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for NLCS Game 4

Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive. Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots.
Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive.
Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both contributed to the Dodgers' lone run-scoring rally in the sixth inning, with Ohtani drawing a walk to load the bases before Smith cashed in with a two-run double. Two innings later, Ohtani smoked a 113.5 mph single, his hardest-hit batted ball since June 20.
The big plate appearances from Ohtani and Smith, as well as the work they have put in behind the scenes, were enough to convince manager Dave Roberts to elevate both of them back up the order.
"I think getting back to what we've done all year and how it's been going recently as far as on the offense," Roberts said, "I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup."
Here's the full lineup:
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernández, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernández, 3B
The Dodgers are trying to do what just one other team has done before: Come back from being down 0-3 in a best-of-seven postseason series. Of the 42 teams that have been in that position, only Roberts' 2004 Red Sox have successfully come back to win the series. Thirty-two of those series ended in sweeps.
Roberts' advice to his team is to focus solely on winning Game 4. They can't look at the big picture of needing four wins in as many games. They need to win each pitch, each inning and each day for as long as their season is alive.
Having Ohtani back atop the order, Roberts hopes, will put the Dodgers in the best position to do that. Ohtani is hitting 4-for-22 (.182) with no extra-base hits, seven strikeouts and four walks in seven games this postseason. There was a discussion about sitting him for Game 3 amid his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries, but Ohtani was adamant that he felt good enough to play and was close to figuring something out with his swing.
The reasoning for Ohtani's return to the leadoff spot a game later is twofold: He showed Roberts enough through his work and in Game 3. And if this is it for the Dodgers' postseason run, Roberts wants to go down trusting his generational talent to set the tone.
"There is something to that, absolutely," Roberts said. "But also I think the player still has to give you hope to believe in, to bet on -- where I think that the work, being here till 9 p.m. two nights ago working, the at-bats yesterday. For me baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top."

They managed just two runs in Game 3 of the NLCS, the first of three potential games in Los Angeles. Who is Pitching For the Dodgers? As they announced before the start of the series, the Dodgers have Tyler Glasnow on the mound for the fourth game of the NLC
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers set their lineup for their NLCS Game 4 matchup against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday.
The Dodgers currently face a 3-0 deficit in the series, and need to win Thursday’s game to keep their World Series hopes alive. They managed just two runs in Game 3 of the NLCS, the first of three potential games in Los Angeles.
Who is Pitching For the Dodgers?
As they announced before the start of the series, the Dodgers have Tyler Glasnow on the mound for the fourth game of the NLCS. Injuries cut Glasnow’s regular season short, allowing him to make just 22 starts while posting a 3.49 ERA, but he earned an all-important win for the team in Game 4 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.
He threw 4.2 innings while allowing just one earned run, though he allowed five walks in the process. The veteran right-hander will look to keep the Brewers off of the board to give the Dodgers some kind of advantage in Thursday’s game.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers made just one substitution in their lineup from Game 3, but drastically changed the order in which their hitters appear. Shohei Ohtani returned to the top of the lineup as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, followed by shortstop Mookie Betts and first baseman Freddie Freeman. Catcher Will Smith, after his two-run double in Wednesday’s loss, returns to the cleanup spot for the Dodgers, and right fielder Kyle Tucker follows him to the plate.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez will bat sixth, and Miguel Rojas remains in the lineup, though as the second baseman for Game 4. Batting eighth is center fielder Andy Pages, and Kiké Hernandez steps in at third base to round out the lineup.
Dodgers’ Lineup vs. Braves
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernandez, 3B
P. Tyler Glasnow, RHP.
When Does Thursday’s Game Start?
First pitch for Thursday’s game comes at 5:00 p.m. PT, moved up one hour from the original start time of 6:00 p.m. PT due to scheduling changes in the ALDS. The Dodgers will look to generate some offense and extend their season with a strong performance in Game 4.

item.content:encoded:
On Day 5 of the League Championship Series, one team broke a series tie ... will another advance to the Fall Classic?
After splitting the first two games in Tampa Bay, the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays faced off at Progressive Field in the day's first game. Thanks toPetey Halpin-- and his epic bat flip -- Cleveland prevailed, taking a 2-1 ALCS lead.
Tonight, in what could be the finale of the NLCS, the Milwaukee Brewers will look to continue their dominant championship series run and sweep the reigning champion Los Angeles Dodgers at Dodger Stadium. Can the Dodgers stave off elimination in Game 4 -- or will the Brewers advance to their first World Series since 1982?
Stay tuned for in-game action and postgame analysis from Los Angeles and Cleveland.
Key links: How final four teams were built | Playoff MVP tracker | Schedule
Cleveland leads series 2-1
It was over when ... Petey Halpin cranked a 96 mph sinker down the middle from Griffin Jax in the fifth inning. The ball landed deep into the right-field seats, 385 feet away, for a go-ahead two-run home run. Halpin flipped his bat nearly that high, too, and Cleveland didn't look back.
Game 3 star: Halpin, who began the season in Triple-A, had four big league home runs -- all during the regular season -- in 213 career plate appearances before Thursday. The center fielder's first postseason homer was the difference Thursday.
The stat that defined the game:The Rays' 13 strikeouts against Guardians pitching. The Rays posted the lowest strikeout rate in the majors this season at 18.8%. They struck out more than 12 times once, when they compiled 14 strikeouts against the Milwaukee Brewers back on March 30 in their fourth game of the season. Rays star Junior Caminero went 0-for-4 with four strikeouts -- matching a career high from 2025. So Thursday was an extreme outlier. Guardians starter Gavin Williams, the American League's strikeout leader this season, had nine strikeouts in five innings before four relievers combined for the remaining four punchouts. Tampa Bay will have to put the ball in play more to come back and win this series.
What it means for the rest of the series: With rain in the forecast Friday, there's a chance this series won't play Game 4 until Saturday. If so, the clubs would play Game 5 on Sunday, which would take away their travel day before a potential Game 6 in Tampa Bay on Monday. For now, Game 4 is scheduled for 6 p.m. ET Friday. -- Jorge Castillo
Highlights from the Guardians' win:
Halpin's homer, um, flips lead back to Guardians
Simpson silences Cleveland crowd with two-run triple
Gavin gettin' it done early
Guardians score first on Lowe's double
A series-defining day?

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Pat Murphy's Managing Masterclass Outshines Dave Roberts, Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: The 2026 National League Championship Series has been all Milwaukee Brewers so far. Milwaukee has a commanding three-game lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers with Game 4 scheduled to be played on Thursday night. If the Brewers win, they will advance to the World Series. There were many who thought the Brewers' streak of winning the National League Central would come to an end this season. Instead, the Brewers are on the doorstep of history. There are many reasons why Milwaukee has outplayed the Do
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 National League Championship Series has been all Milwaukee Brewers so far.
Milwaukee has a commanding three-game lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers with Game 4 scheduled to be played on Thursday night. If the Brewers win, they will advance to the World Series.
There were many who thought the Brewers' streak of winning the National League Central would come to an end this season. Instead, the Brewers are on the doorstep of history. There are many reasons why Milwaukee has outplayed the Dodgers throughout the series. The bullpen has been incredible, Jake Bauers has shined and the rotation has done its job. One guy who deserves a lot of credit is Pat Murphy, as well.
There's a reason why he's the two-time reigning National League Manager of the Year and should win the award again. Murphy has pushed all of the right buttons throughout the NLCS. Between the Brewers and the Dodgers, the NLCS has two of the best managers in the game in Murphy and Dave Roberts. Of the two, Murphy has clearly been the best this series, though.
The Brewers Are Sitting Pretty
It seems like every single decision the Brewers have made this series has been the right one. In Game 2, the Brewers put David Hamilton in the starting lineup and he went 2-for-3 with three runs scored and two stolen bases. That was a game-changer. In Game 1, the Brewers had Luis Lara in the starting lineup and he drove in what would end up being the game-winning run for Milwaukee. In Game 3, the Brewers started the game with Christian Yelich, Sal Frelick and Hamilton all on the bench. Andrew Vaughn, who replaced Yelich in the lineup, drew an important walk in the seventh inning. Then, Yelich pinch-ran for him and was driven in by Bauers' two-run homer.
Ortiz, who was at third base over Hamilton, drove in a run during the Game 3 win as well. Plus, the Brewers have gotten seemingly every pitching decision right. The starters haven't gone deep and Milwaukee has known exactly when to turn it over to the bullpen. On the other hand, Roberts made what could be argued as a few mistakes, specifically in Game 3. Andy Pages was yanked in favor of Max Muncy. Prized rookie Josue De Paula was wasted in Game 3 as well and was replaced by Kiké Hernandez at a critical point in the game. Plus, the offense in general has done nothing.
Milwaukee has pushed all of the right buttons, whereas the Dodgers have faltered. This is absolutely a testament to Murphy, as well as the players on the field.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding "Milwaukee Brewers On SI," please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

So we gotta go on
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers’ Game 3 NLCS loss to the Brewers on Wednesday hit hard for fans and players alike.
Beloved Dodgers utilityman Kiké Hernández seemed to take this loss especially tough, given how he looked when speaking to the media postgame.
“We didn’t expect to be in this situation, this position. But this one sucks,” Hernández said, per Santiago Gil Sam.
“We’ve got to find a way to turn the page quick, because tomorrow is gonna be here pretty fast. And, yeah. We lose, we’re done. So we gotta go on one-game winning streaks for four games in a row and see what happens. But, yeah, this one sucks,” he added.
Hernández’s eyes were noticeably watery throughout the interview, and he looked like he was about to cry when realizing that the Dodgers likely lost their one opportunity to salvage this NLCS.
Hernández doesn’t need to be reminded that history has not boded well for MLB teams down 3-0 in a series. Only one of 43 teams has won a series from this position, and Los Angeles’ uninspired performance to this point doesn’t make it seem like they will be No. 2.
The 35-year-old Hernández hasn’t tallied a hit in five NLCS at-bats. He’ll be a free agent after this season, which could mean Thursday will be his last game wearing a Dodgers uniform.
Perhaps that played in to his emotional reaction to Los Angeles’ Game 3 defeat.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] MLB Playoff Roundup: Bauers leads Brewers’ blasts on brink of World Series

item.content:encoded:
Is this finally the year the Brewers exorcise their playoff demons and advance past the Dodgers on the Senior Circuit side of the bracket? Alongside LA, Milwaukee has been the class of the NL regular season for the last decade. However, they have never beaten their postseason final boss during this era, getting eliminated by the Dodgers in seven games in the instant classic 2018 NLCS before getting swept in the 2020 NL Wild Card Series and 2025 NLCS.
MLB Playoff Roundup: Bauers leads Brewers’ blasts on brink of World Series
Milwaukee is on the cusp of sweeping the Dodgers and making their second World Series appearance in franchise history.
That finally looks set to change, the Brewers taking a commanding 3-0 lead in the series on a brilliant start from Robert Gasser and home runs from Jackson Chourio, Jake Bauers, and Garrett Mitchell. With one more win, they’ll not only avenge those losses, but also win their first pennant in 44 years, when Harvey’s Wallbangers led the 1982 Brewers to the AL flag. Only the Pirates and Mariners have waited longer for a World Series berth. Could this be the year at last for dreams of a first Brewers championship to truly ignite?
They have one more win to go. Here’s how they got to the doorstep.
NLCS Game 3
Milwaukee Brewers 5, Los Angeles Dodgers 2
(Milwaukee leads, 3-0)
There is no better start to the game as a visiting team than a leadoff home run to put the home starter and crowd immediately on the back foot. Chourio said “hold my beer” as he homered on the first pitch of Game 3, ambushing a center-cut four-seamer from Blake Snell and lining it oppo just over the wall in right-center to instantly deflate a raucous crowd at Chavez Ravine who had been desperate to energize their wounded Dodgers. It is already the third postseason leadoff home run in the young career of the Brewers’ star left fielder, Chourio the hero of the NLDS against the Padres with six RBIs in four games.
Gasser typifies a Milwaukee Brewers player — a gamer with plenty of talent but not a name a baseball fan outside of Wisconsin is likely to recognize. He was part of the 2022 deadline trade that sent Josh Hader to San Diego. He debuted in 2024 but missed most of that and the next season to Tommy John surgery. He spent the first month-and-a-half of 2026 at Triple-A but didn’t look back after a mid-May call-up, starting 20 games and posting a 5-5 record, 3.87 ERA, 4.23 FIP, 103 strikeouts and 1.5 fWAR in 109.1 innings.
With the Brewers unsettled on their postseason rotation plans, Gasser allowed one or fewer runs in his final four starts of the regular season to cement his starting role in the playoffs. The 27-year-old lefty held the Padres to a run on three hits in four innings of Game 4 of the NLDS as the Brewers punched their ticket to the next round. Against this backdrop of hitting his stride once the games really started to matter, Gasser pitched possibly the best start of his life last night.
He’s not going to blow you away with velocity, but the unique way he hides the ball until the last moment of his delivery let his mid-90s sinker play up in LA. The Dodgers had no answer for the pitch as Gasser was able to paint both sides of the plate, getting the ball by the dangerous hitters in their lineup as if they collectively were not ready to hit the fastball.
Gasser waltzed through five scoreless innings allowing just three hits and a walk, but cameras curiously spotted handshakes in the dugout between the fifth and sixth innings. Gasser hadn’t had to make a stressful pitch all game and seemed to have plenty in the tank at just 72 pitches, but trainers did appear to be tending to a blister on the ring finger of his pitching hand. Practically every button that Brewers manager Pat Murphy has pushed this season and postseason has worked, seeing the team pace MLB with 103 wins and easily brush aside the Padres in the NLDS before taking a 2-0 lead over the two-time reigning champions, but this one blew up in his face.
Whatever the case, Murphy called on Abner Uribe for the sixth inning and it backfired spectacularly. He walked Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker, and Shohei Ohtani (batting a rare sixth amid his awful slump) to load the bases with one out. Despite a pair of relievers hot in the Milwaukee bullpen, Murphy allowed Uribe to face the struggling Will Smith — 1-for-23 in six games this postseason. Smith ambushed a first pitch sinker right down the pipe, the deep fly ball clanging halfway up the wall in left-center to plate a pair and give the Dodgers their first lead of the series, 2-1.
Murphy belatedly called on flame throwing lefty DL Hall to clean up Uribe’s mess, and he struck out Kiké Hernández and Tommy Edman to strand runners on second and third and limit the damage to the two runs.
Murphy was perhaps vindicated in lifting his starter earlier than it seemed necessary, because we witnessed the flip side of that debate two innings later. It is perhaps fitting that Snell was the starter opposite Gasser in this game —the Rays’ Kevin Cash memorably removed Snell in the sixth inning of Game 6 of the 2020 World Series against the Dodgers despite Snell having struck out nine and not allowed a run on just 73 pitches — Gasser removed with his pitch count at 72.
After the Chourio leadoff blast, Snell was untouchable for six innings, allowing one hit and one walk while striking out nine as his four-seamer had some extra juice en route to racking up a gaudy 46-percent whiff rate. Dave Roberts allowed his dominating starter to come back out for the seventh, and it is amazing how the tide turned in an instant. He issued a leadoff walk to Andrew Vaughn, but with two lefties due up in Bauers and Mitchell, Roberts stuck with his southpaw starter.
The fatigue was apparent against Bauers, Snell’s misses occurring over the heart of the plate instead of outside of the zone, and the Brewers’ regular season home run leader won the monumental 11-pitch battle by blasting a middle-middle full count four-seamer 412 feet to right to put the Brewers back on top, 3-2. Mitchell then jumped on a 1-0 mistake changeup right down the middle, going back-to-back with Bauers to almost the exact same spot of the ballpark.
It was the first time in Snell’s entire career that he had allowed back-to-back homers to lefties and just the second time that he’d ever allowed two lefty-hitter homers in the same game (let alone inning). He’d allowed one lefty-hitter homer since Juan Soto took him deep for the Yankees in June 2024 in San Francisco.
That fully sucked all of the air out of Dodger Stadium, and the team nor their fans could will the comeback. Milwaukee added a pair of valuable insurance runs in the eighth and ninth. Brice Turang and William Contreras reached in the eighth on consecutive one-out singles to put runners on the corners where a Justin Wrobleski wild pitch allowed Turang to score the Brewers’ fifth run. Rookie Cooper Pratt lined a one-out single in the ninth, stole second, and scored on a Joey Ortiz single to make it 6-2. Hall and closer Trevor Megill combined to pitch a scoreless final 3.2 innings to seal the win and put the Brewers on the brink of sweeping the champions of the last two seasons.
Game 4 is tomorrow with first pitch scheduled for 8:00 pm ET. Tyler Glasnow will look to keep the Dodgers’ season alive while Milwaukee has yet to name a starter. The Brewers now have four chances to clinch the series and advance to the Fall Classic, where they will look to win their first ever title as one of five teams to have never won a ring. No expansion team has waited longer. It may finally be the Brew Crew’s year.

item.title: [1069thefox.com] Brewers stun Dodgers with back-to-back homers in 7th inning and ride 6-2 win to 3-0 lead in NLCS - 106.9 The Fox
