item.content:encoded:
By BETH HARRIS AP Sports Writer
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Milwaukee Brewers hit the second-fewest home runs in baseball during the regular season, even as they topped the majors with 103 wins.
Maybe they were saving their biggest swings for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell launched back-to-back homers off Blake Snell in the seventh inning, and the Brewers beat the Dodgers 6-2 on Wednesday to build a 3-0 cushion in the National League Championship Series.
Jackson Chourio also went deep on the first pitch of the game to help the Brewers close within one win of their first NL pennant. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise reached its only World Series, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals in 1982.
“Job’s not finished yet,” Mitchell said.
Game 4 is Thursday at Dodger Stadium, where the Brewers can become the first major league club to complete a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
Los Angeles took all four games against Milwaukee in the NLCS last year.
The Dodgers had just gone ahead 2-1 in the sixth inning before getting stunned by the Brewers in their three-run seventh. The loss pushed the two-time defending World Series champions to the brink of elimination.
“All three games we’ve played so far, and hopefully that continues, where just every time they score, we come back and score,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. “That’s not easy to do in baseball.”
It was the fifth comeback victory in seven postseason games for the Brewers, who have never beaten Los Angeles in three previous playoff series.
The only other time the Dodgers trailed 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, they were swept by the Baltimore Orioles in the 1966 World Series.
The lone team in big league history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven postseason series was the Boston Red Sox in the 2004 AL Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “We’ve got to win tomorrow. That’s our only focus.”
Coming into the seventh, Snell had retired 14 batters in a row. But the first pitch of the game thrown by the two-time Cy Young Award winner was hit for a home run by Chourio, and his last pitch was Mitchell’s solo shot.
Andrew Vaughn drew a seven-pitch walk to open the seventh and was replaced by pinch-runner Christian Yelich. Bauers followed with a 412-foot drive to right field on the 11th pitch of his at-bat for a 3-2 lead as most of the players in Milwaukee’s dugout came onto the field to celebrate.
“I was looking for a fastball, and I didn’t want to miss it,” said Bauers, who had a team-leading 26 of Milwaukee’s 154 regular-season homers.
It was his latest relentless plate appearance, too, after Bauers drew a 12-pitch walk from Yoshinobu Yamamoto that helped the Brewers go ahead early in Game 2.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results,” Bauers said. “I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
Watching Bauers work over Snell was “super sick,” Mitchell said.
And then it was his turn.
Mitchell’s drive traveled 428 feet to right-center. That chased Snell, who hadn’t given up a home run in 46 1/3 innings this year entering the game. It was the first time in his career he served up back-to-back homers to left-handed hitters and only the second time he gave up multiple longballs to left-handed batters in one game.
Bauers and Mitchell became just the third pair of left-handed hitters with consecutive postseason home runs off the same left-handed pitcher. Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper did it for Philadelphia against Atlanta reliever Dylan Lee in an NL Wild Card Series this year, and Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig connected for the New York Yankees off Bill Sherdel of the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1928 World Series.
Milwaukee has five homers in the NLCS and eight this postseason.
Snell gave up four runs and four hits in six-plus innings. He struck out nine and walked two.
The Brewers extended their lead to 5-2 in the eighth on Justin Wrobleski’s wild pitch that scored Brice Turang, who reached on an infield single and advanced to third on William Contreras’ single. They added another run on Joey Ortiz’s two-strike RBI single in the ninth.
The offensively starved Dodgers took a 2-1 lead on Will Smith’s two-run double off reliever Abner Uribe in the sixth.
After rookie starter Robert Gasser pitched five shutout innings, Uribe entered and loaded the bases on walks to Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker and Shohei Ohtani. Smith, who was 1 for 25 in the playoffs, doubled off the left-center fence with one out for his first hit of the NLCS.
DL Hall took over from Uribe and stranded runners at second and third by striking out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernández and Tommy Edman.
Hall allowed one hit in 2 1/3 scoreless innings to improve to 3-0 in these playoffs. Trevor Megill got four outs for his second save of the series and fourth this postseason.
The Dodgers played from behind again after the 22-year-old Chourio connected for his third career leadoff homer in the postseason as fans were still heading to their seats.
After that, Mitchell walked and Cooper Pratt singled in the second before Snell retired 14 in a row — six on strikeouts — before getting hammered in the seventh.
The Dodgers had runners on base in all but three innings, but couldn’t get enough across. They have yet to homer in the NLCS and are 3 for 32 with runners in scoring position this postseason.
Ohtani was 1 for 2 with a walk while hitting sixth in the order, the lowest he’s batted since joining the Dodgers three years ago.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dave Roberts' Blake Snell decision was the tip of the iceberg in mortifying Dodgers Game 3 loss
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: Dave Roberts has not been at his best in the NLCS, with the Los Angeles Dodgers facing the league-best Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-seven that's making LA's NLDS against the Atlanta Braves look like the smallest of potatoes. In Game 2, Roberts had Brock Stewart intentionally walk Brice Turang in the sixth to get to the Brewers' hottest hitter in William Contreras, for seemingly no other reason than that the righty-righty matchup looked favorable on paper. item.content:encoded:
Dave Roberts has not been at his best in the NLCS, with the Los Angeles Dodgers facing the league-best Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-seven that's making LA's NLDS against the Atlanta Braves look like the smallest of potatoes.
In Game 2, Roberts had Brock Stewart intentionally walk Brice Turang in the sixth to get to the Brewers' hottest hitter in William Contreras, for seemingly no other reason than that the righty-righty matchup looked favorable on paper. Contreras hit a go-ahead single on the first pitch Stewart served him.
That was small potatoes in contrast to Game 3, where Roberts seemed to make the worst possible decision at every conceivable turn. There is, of course, leaving Blake Snell in after he walked Andrew Vaughn to lead off the seventh, which then turned into a go-ahead, two-run homer for Jake Bauers ... and then a solo homer for Garrett Mitchell for some insurance.
The Dodgers went down 6-2, and their backs are now firmly against the wall. Roberts' Snell decision is the one that's going to be remembered least fondly, but there was a parade of other choices that all but doomed LA's three-peat hopes.
Dave Roberts' Blake Snell decision is obscuring smaller mistakes that doomed the Dodgers in NLCS Game 3
Roberts' next greatest sin, perhaps, was burning Josue De Paula in the bottom of the sixth. After Will Smith broke out of his slumber to hit a bases-loaded, go-ahead double, Roberts replaced Miguel Rojas with left Josue De Paula to face righty Abner Uribe. Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy countered by bringing in lefty DL Hall, so Roberts figured he would do play 3D chess and instead offered up righty Kiké Hernández, rendering De Paula unavailable for the rest of the game. Hernández struck out swinging.
There's the fact that Roberts started Tommy Edman, who had a single hit coming into Game 3. He went 0-for-4 on Wednesday night. There's the fact that he put Justin Wrobleski, who had a 6.13 ERA in the second half and was briefly demoted to Triple-A, in the game with the Dodgers down by two. Wrobleski quickly threw a wild pitch that allowed the Brewers' fifth run to score.
It might be going a little too far to say that this showing was legacy-threatening ... but it sure does feel like that right now. Roberts, no doubt, will be appropriately self-critical if the Dodgers' postseason road comes to an end after this series, but that doesn't erase how inexplicable his decisions in Game 3 were, and that they, alone, might've doomed LA.

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
Blake Snell stood on the mound with his hand on his hip, waiting for Jake Bauers to cross the plate before punching in his pitch call for the next batter.
The Dodgers left-hander had just given up the lead on Bauers’ two-run homer, spoiling what had been a stellar start Wednesday night at Dodger Stadium. But Snell was ready to move on.
Two pitches later, he watched another ball fly over the fence, this time off Garrett Mitchell’s bat.
The Dodgers’ 6-2 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, after the visitors regained the lead with back-to-back home runs in the seventh inning, gave the Brewers a commanding 3-0 lead and set up an elimination game Thursday. After setting their sights on a history-making three-peat, the Dodgers will have to win the next four games just to advance to the World Series.
The Dodgers showed signs of life during Game 3 of the NLCS, but Bill Plaschke writes the reigning champs can’t survive their crushing collapse.
For five innings, the only run on the board was the one the Brewers scored on the first pitch of the game.
Snell zipped a 97.6-mph fastball over the center of the plate, and Brewers leadoff hitter Jackson Chourio sent it into the first row of the stands in right-center.
For much of Snell’s start, however, that aggressive approach worked. He dotted the upper rail with his fastball, threw his curveball for both swings and misses and called strikes, and mixed in his changeup to right-handed batters.
Unlike Snell’s last postseason start, when he issued five walks and lasted just 3-2/3 innings against the Atlanta Braves, his efficiency got him through six-plus innings Wednesday, with just two walks.
And while Snell’s fastball averaged 97 mph in his last start — something he’d done only twice before in his career, regular season or postseason, and not since 2022, according to Statcast — he threw even harder on Wednesday: 97.3 mph.
After Chourio’s home run, Snell retired 18 of the next 20 batters, including 14 in a row, to get through six innings. His nine strikeouts were one shy of a postseason career high, which he recorded against the Brewers last year in Game 1 of the NLCS.
Then in the seventh inning, he issued a leadoff walk to Andrew Vaughn and surrendered back-to-back homers, and suddenly the game had flipped.
With the way the Brewers’ bullpen pitched in the first two games, it seemed the Dodgers would have to score against the Brewers’ starters to have a chance to pull themselves out of the hole they’d dug.
They failed to do so in Game 3, logging just three hits off left-hander Robert Gasser.
Luckily for them, pitching every game of the postseason seemed to finally have caught up to hard-throwing right-handed Abner Uribe in his seventh appearance.
Uribe took over for Gasser in the sixth inning and walked the first two batters he faced.
Then Dodgers manager Dave Roberts had left-handed-hitting Max Muncy pinch-hit for Andy Pages. Muncy struck out, and the biggest moment of the game fell to two Dodgers who have had the worst postseason production on the team.
Roberts had moved Shohei Ohtani down to sixth in the batting order and put Will Smith behind him. Naturally, the game found them.
Ohtani drew a five-pitch walk without taking a swing. With the bases loaded, it was up to Smith, who had gone one for 25 in the postseason to that point.
He ambushed a first-pitch sinker and drove it into the left-field gap for a two-run double and the lead.
The rally halted there. Roberts burned rookie Josue De Paula as a pinch-hitter, swapping him out for Kiké Hernández when the Brewers brought in left-hander DL Hall. Hernández and Tommy Edman struck out to end the inning.
The Dodgers could not keep pace with the Milwaukee Brewers, falling 6-2 Wednesday night in Game 3 of the NLCS and dropping to 3-0 in the series.
Then, three Brewers batters into the seventh, the Dodgers were down 4-2.
Snell hadn’t allowed a home run all year — not in his nine regular-season starts, or in his NLDS appearance. Three on Wednesday defined his start.
The next inning, the Brewers added an insurance run with back-to-back singles against right-handed reliever Roki Sasaki and a wild pitch from left-hander Justin Wrobleski. They tacked on another in the ninth with a pair of singles and a stolen base off Wrobleski.
With the flash of red tail lights flickering outside of the stadium, a sign of Dodgers fans already heading for the exits, Dodgers hitters went down in order in the final half inning.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Brewers push Dodgers to the brink, hit 3 homers off Blake Snell for 3-0 NLCS lead
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Reach out and feel the drywall. The Dodgers’ backs are up against it.
The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. The Milwaukee Brewers handed the Dodgers a 6-2 defeat in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, pushing the back-to-back champions to the brink of elimination with the possibility of a sweep to avenge the one the Dodgers handed them last year.
“It’s a pretty simple answer,” Max Muncy said when asked how the Dodgers find themselves in this position. “We’re playing like (profanity). They’re playing great. It’s as simple as that. No need to overcomplicate it.”
Dreams of a three-peat on life support, the Dodgers’ thoughts now have to be on a ‘four-peat’ – it will take four consecutive victories for them to become just the second team in MLB history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven series. The 2004 Boston Red Sox (featuring a key stolen base by a reserve outfielder acquired at midseason from the Dodgers) did it in the American League Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“If we lose, we’re done. We’ve got to go on one-game winning streaks four games in a row,” Kike’ Hernandez said.
“At the beginning of this year, we set out to do something historic,” Muncy said. “It looks like we’re going to have to make a little more history along the way if we want to accomplish that. That’s the task ahead of us. We still have the pitching staff to be able to do it. We just have to get some hits. If we can back our pitching staff then I know that, like I said, we have the pitching staff to do it.”
Tyler Glasnow is scheduled to start Game 4 on Thursday and try to save the Dodgers’ season. Muncy is correct — Glasnow won’t be able to do it without someone applying paddles to the Dodgers’ flatlining offense.
The Dodgers might not be going down without a fight. But so far, they are going down without any of the things it takes to make an offense successful in the postseason.
They are 2 for 16 with runners in scoring position in this series, 3 for 32 in the postseason. They have just two two-out hits in the three NLCS games (both singles) and only two extra-base hits (both doubles). The Dodgers hit 204 home runs in the regular season (tied for fourth in the National League) and eight more in their four-game National League Division Series victory over the Atlanta Braves (the most in the postseason to that point). They have hit none in the NLCS.
“They’re really good pitchers,” Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard. They’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too many opportunities to build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They trust their stuff in the zone. With all three fastballs, with a lot of guys that have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball, it’s really hard to kind of put barrels on the ball. So you’ve got to build some momentum that you can create with hits, but we haven’t been able to get a big hit.”
The Brewers have grabbed any momentum right back from the Dodgers. The Dodgers have scored in just five of the 27 innings so far. Four of those five times, the Brewers responded by scoring in the next half-inning themselves.
It happened again to turn Game 3.
Snell hadn’t give up a home run this year but Jackson Chourio sent the first pitch he threw Wednesday into the right-field pavilion. Snell thoroughly dominated the Brewers through six innings after that. He retired 18 of 20 batters after Chourio’s home run, striking out nine. Through the first five innings, the Brewers swung at 32 of Snell’s pitches and missed (17) more times than they made contact.
But the Dodgers’ lifeless offense did nothing against the Brewers’ second consecutive rookie starter, Robert Gasser, who held them scoreless on three hits and a walk through five innings.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy went to his bullpen after that, calling on Abner Uribe for the seventh time in their seven postseason games. When Uribe took the mound, the Brewers’ relievers had pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings in the NLCS and had allowed just one earned run in 28⅔ innings this postseason.
But Uribe walked the bases loaded, retiring just one batter. That brought up Will Smith – 1 for his first 25 this postseason. Smith jumped on a first-pitch fastball from Uribe and lined it off the wall in left-center field for a two-run double and a 2-1 lead.
It was the kind of clutch hit that Smith has provided time and time again over the years and had the stadium rocking.
Murphy made his next move, bringing in left-hander DL Hall with runners at second and third. Hall struck out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernandez and Tommy Edman as the Dodgers failed to capitalize on a chance to break the game open.
Snell went back out for the seventh inning having retired 14 in a row. But he walked Andrew Vaughn to start the inning and bring up Jake Bauers whose 12-pitch walk in the third inning of Game 2 was a critical turning point against Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He did it again, extending his at-bat against Snell for 11 pitches and sending the last one, a fastball over the heart of the plate, into the right-field seats for a two-run home run. Two pitches later, Snell floated a changeup over the middle and Garrett Mitchell sent it on the same flight path as Bauers’ drive.
In 1,200⅔ career innings (regular season), Snell has only given up 15 home runs to left-handed hitters. Bauers and Mitchell did it back-to-back. The Brewers hit 154 home runs during the regular season, the fewest in the National League. They have outhomered the Dodgers 5-0 in the NLCS.
“I mean three home runs in a game — I didn’t give up one the whole year,” Snell said. “To have three in a game is pretty frustrating.”
The Brewers added single runs in the eighth and ninth innings to pull away.

item.title: [New York Post] Mookie Betts could be the answer to the Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani problem
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez

Betts was the best player on the 2020 championship team. He finished in the top five in National League MVP voting three of his first four seasons with the Dodgers. Now, with the Dodgers trailing the Brewers in the National League Championship Series and unable to count on a physically-limited Ohtani to jumpstart their offense, Betts will have to tu
item.content:encoded:
Before the Dodgers became Shohei Ohtani’s team, they were Mookie Betts’ team.
Manager Dave Roberts used to say that as Betts went, the Dodgers went.
Betts was the best player on the 2020 championship team. He finished in the top five in National League MVP voting three of his first four seasons with the Dodgers.
Now, with the Dodgers trailing the Brewers in the National League Championship Series and unable to count on a physically-limited Ohtani to jumpstart their offense, Betts will have to turn back the clock.
The Dodgers scored only once in the first game of the NLCS and each of the four runs they scored in the second game was the result of an error or wild pitch by the Brewers, but Betts can’t be faulted for the lack of run production.
Betts, who replaced Ohtani as the leadoff hitter last month while the four-time MVP was on the injured list, was 2-for-7 through the first two games of the NLCS.
He reached base four times in nine plate appearances.
“Mookie’s at-bats at the top, and what he’s done over the last couple months has been very consistent,” Roberts said. “It’s at-bat quality at the highest level.”
The effect of those at-bats on the Dodgers’ other hitters was particularly obvious in a victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of their NL Division Series.
In his first at-bat against Braves ace Chris Sale, Betts laid off a slider that just missed the lower outside corner of the plate to work the count full. On the next pitch Betts reached base on an infield single.
“Really just trying to have good at-bats and try to not have a bunch of empty one-out flyouts,” Betts said.
The Dodgers forced Sale to throw 24 pitches in the first inning. By the end of the third inning, Sale’s pitch count was already at 69. In the fourth inning, the Dodgers struck, with home runs by Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman moving them in front, 3-0.
The Dodgers went on to win the game, 3-1, and Betts finished with two hits.
“When you’re getting into a playoff series and you get that first hitter seeing pitches, it sets the tone for the rest of the lineup, and also for that starting pitcher that it’s going to be a grindy day,” Roberts said.
Against the Brewers, the Dodgers face an entirely different kind of challenge. The strength of the Brewers is their bullpen.
“I don’t know that it’s super imperative for us to run up the pitch counts or anything because the back end of their bullpen is arguably better than everybody on the team,” Betts said. “Getting to them isn’t necessarily a huge success.”
Unless Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski is pitching for the Brewers, the Dodgers’ prime scoring opportunities to score could be against their starting pitchers.
“Really scoring runs when you can,” Betts said.
Betts described the Dodgers as being in a good headspace.
“Nobody is really panicking or anything,” he said. “Obviously we know it’s a tough task. It’s a really good ball club over there. We just have to start one game, one pitch at a time.”
Betts said he didn’t see a reason for the team to be discouraged.
“It’s not like we’re playing really bad,” he said. “I think we’re just not getting the hits that we need to really explode as an offense. One hit can kind of lead to two and then kind of keep us going.”
The Dodgers were also in trouble in each of their last two World Series runs – they were behind two-games-to-one against the San Diego Padres in their best-of-five NL Division Series in 2024; and they trailed three games to two against the Toronto Blue Jays in the World Series last year.
“I think just having that experience, that’s kind of what gives us encouragement,” Betts said. “Being that we’ve been here before and we got out of it keeps us in a really good head space.
“Obviously, every year is different, but the same rules apply. We’ve got to just keep playing the game, and that’s really it.”

item.content:encoded:
Alex Call didn't get the call to help his Los Angeles Dodgers survive October, but one thing off the field has bothered him enough to call out MLB publicly.
Sydney Sweeney's revealing Novig commercial has pushed him over the edge. The LA outfielder tagged MLB, TBS, Fox, and NBC in a post asking them to remove what he called “soft p--- ads” from postseason broadcasts.
Call said the issue hit him while he was watching baseball with his young son and wondering what ad might suddenly appear during a commercial break. The 32-year-old was left off the Dodgers' active NLDS and NLCS squads but remains on the team's active 40-man roster.
His post argued MLB did not need gimmicks to attract younger viewers, just a broadcast that families could comfortably keep on. "Can we please get the soft p--- ads off playoff broadcasts, TBS, Fox, NBC, MLB?" he wrote.
"My son wants to watch baseball with Dada, but how do I justify that when a half-naked woman could come on screen anytime? This is America’s Pastime. Parents shouldn’t have to worry about this."
Call was responding to another parent who complained that a playoff broadcast included an erectile dysfunction commercial featuring Megan Fox and Sweeney's Novig spot, backed by company owners.
Advertisement
Sweeney is the face of Novig's “Just Sports” campaign, and the "Euphoria" actress appears nude or nearly nude in several versions, using footballs and other sports equipment to cover herself while delivering the “it's Just Sports” punchline.
The campaign was meant to be provocative and has since been updated, with Sweeney again topless, using footballs and her hair for cover.
Female athletes and commentators have criticized the concept for objectifying women in sports, while Sweeney and Novig defend the campaign as playful marketing centered on the company's sports-only pitch.
The actress also holds an undisclosed equity ownership stake in the company. Los Angeles has deployed both Teoscar Hernandez and Kike Hernández primarily at left field during the postseason.
Los Angeles entered Wednesday's NLCS Game 3 against Milwaukee down 2-0 after dropping the first two road games.
The Dodgers are trying to defend back-to-back World Series championships, with every October broadcast under watchful eyes. Call hit .233 with one home run and 20 RBI across 88 regular-season games in 2026.
He has been married to his wife, Samantha, since 2019, and the couple has been together since attending Ball State University from 2014 to 2016.

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers losing both Enrique Hernandez, Teoscar Hernandez to IL

Teoscar Hernandez pulled up lame while running to first base in Wednesday's second inning and was diagnosed with a l
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers placed super-utility man Enrique Hernandez on the injured list Wednesday and will do the same with left fielderTeoscar Hernandez the next time they play Friday.
Enrique Hernandez suffered what Dodgers manager Dave Roberts described as a "significant tear" in his oblique earlier this week, an injury that will keep him out for several weeks, if not months. Teoscar Hernandez pulled up lame while running to first base in Wednesday's second inning and was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, though the initial expectation is that his injury is not as serious.
"He tested well," Roberts said after the Dodgers' 4-1 win over the Colorado Rockies. "But we're going to get a scan tomorrow. Obviously it's an IL. There's just no timeline. But something like that obviously is going to be a few weeks at the minimum."
Enrique Hernandez spent the season's first two months building back up after offseason elbow surgery and suffered the oblique injury while taking batting practice before his season debut Monday. He picked up two hits that night, received treatment Tuesday, homered, then hit a fourth-inning double under significant pain in his left side and was later replaced on defense.
Cameras caught Roberts consoling a visibly shaken Enrique Hernandez in the dugout shortly thereafter.
"I feel pretty defeated right now," Hernandez told reporters after the game.
The Dodgers recalled infield prospect Alex Freeland to fill the vacant roster spot, starting him at second base for the series finale. Freeland will probably get most of the playing time there until Tommy Edman makes his expected return from offseason ankle surgery at some point in June, though Hyeseong Kim will draw starts at second base, too.
The hope is that Enrique Hernandez will at least return for the stretch run of the regular season so he can be a factor in the playoffs, the time of year in which he usually shines. Teoscar Hernandez's stay should be shorter, though it's nonetheless painful for the Dodgers, given his 1.018 OPS over the past 18 games.
"It's pretty frustrating for us," Dodgers center fielder Andy Pages said in Spanish. "We have the opportunity to see them work hard every day and prepare so that those things don't happen. But [injuries are] going to happen all the time."

"De Paula about to be in that upper tie
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers drew six walks during Game 1 of the NLCS, including one from rookie sensation Josue De Paula in the top of the ninth inning.
De Paula pinch-hit for Kiké Hernández with the Dodgeres down 2-1, two outs, and a runner on first base. He drew a five-pitch walk against Milwaukee Brewers closer Trevor Megill, which prompted former Cincinnati Reds great and current NBC analyst Joey Votto to heap praise upon the Dodgers' 21-year-old-prospect.
"De Paula about to be in that upper tier quick, quick.," Votto wrote on X (formerly Twitter) during Sunday's game. In the comments of his tweet, the former MVP went on to mention De Paula's beautiful swing and elite swing-decisions.
The high-end comparison for De Paula has always been Yordan Alvarez, who the Dodgers famously once had in their pipeline. One can assume the likely 2026 AL MVP is certainly a player in Votto's so-called "upper tier" of hitters in MLB. De Paula didn't even swing the bat during his plate appearance in Game 1, but the seeds are being planted for what should be an incredibly successful career.
Dodgers' Josue De Paula is turning heads and could force tough managerial decisions in the playoffs
De Paula now has two walks in his three plate appearances during the postseason. His previous one came during the seventh inning of Game 4 of the NLDS, which allowed the Dodgers to score the go-ahead and game-winning runs to seal the series and advance to the NLCS.
Manager Dave Roberts could swap De Paula for the likes of Hernández, Tommy Edman, or Miguel Rojas. So far, during the postseason, the Dodgers are hitting .207/.282/.360/.642 in the postseason and De Paula's presence on the bench could help alleviate what has been an underwhelming postseason offensively for the reigning back-to-back World Series champions.
It takes every single player on the roster having a clutch moment for a team to win a World Series, and De Paula is showing that he is more than capable of providing an invaluable at bat if he is deployed properly.
De Paula's impressive, yet inconsequential, walk in Game 1 might already have Dodgers fans questioning Teoscar Hernandez's future this offseason. Unless De Paula can learn a new position on the fly like Mookie Betts, he'll completely blocked from the starting lineup by Hernandez, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, in 2027.

item.title: [AOL.com] Bench Shohei Ohtani? Dodgers have to consider drastic action with season in danger - AOL

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– Entering Monday night, the Dodgers were not giving serious consideration to removing Shohei Ohtani from their lineup.
One big loss, and four ugly at-bats later, however, that previously steadfast plan suddenly seemed capable of changing.
Following a 7-4 defeat to the Milwaukee Brewers that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole in their National League Championship Series, the team was set to re-evaluate Ohtani’s status ahead of Game 3 on Wednesday.
Manager Dave Roberts told The Athletic that the team would have “a conversation” with Ohtani about whether or not he would be in the lineup for the contest. A source with knowledge of the situation confirmed to the California Post that the decision would come down to whether Ohtani still felt healthy enough to remain the starting designated hitter, as ESPN also reported.
The development came after Ohtani’s worst performance this postseason, in which he went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts.
Over six games in these playoffs, the four-time MVP is now just 3-for-20 with only three singles, two walks and seven strikeouts while battling ongoing right arm and left knee issues –– playing at what the team has repeatedly acknowledged is well less than 100%.
Despite all that, the Dodgers have also been holding out hope for a revival from their two-way superstar. Roberts promised Ohtani would “come to life” eventually. President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman predicted that “at some point, it’s going to click for him.”
Now, however, the Dodgers might not be able to keep waiting around for Ohtani magic.
After back-to-back losses to open the NLCS in Milwaukee this week, they return home to Los Angeles just two more defeats away from elimination –– and only one from a 3-0 deficit that just one team in MLB history (Roberts’ iconic Boston Red Sox squad in the 2004 American League Championship Series) has ever come back from.
“Can we [come back in this series]? Absolutely,” Roberts said. “But it’s just, you want to get that first [win].”
Prior to Monday, Ohtani had at least reached base safely in each of his first five playoff games.
Instead of continuing to progress with his swing, however, his 0-fer in Game 2 represented a notable step back.
Before the game, the injury-hampered 32-year-old took batting practice on the field for a third-straight day –– a drastic, and telling, change of routine for someone who normally never hits outside of the indoor batting cages.
During his BP sessions, coaches had been encouraged by the look of his swing, optimistically noting the fact he was driving the ball to the big part of the field.
“I feel good [with] where he’s at,” Roberts said Sunday. “[He is] certainly not 100 percent, but it’s good enough.”
Advertisement
That, however, was no longer the case in Tuesday’s demoralizing loss, when the Dodgers’ offense as a whole managed just three hits, made outs in all 15 of their at-bats against Brewers relievers, and suddenly looked like a unit in desperate need of a jolt.
Ohtani didn’t provide one. Instead, he looked even more lost than ever before.
He ended the first inning with a three-pitch strikeout, chasing an elevated fastball from Brewers rookie Logan Henderson. He stranded a runner at second to end the second, flailing at another high fastball for a softly hit grounder to third. Then came the sixth, when Ohtani was so fooled by a slider from left-handed reliever JoJo Romero that his bat flung out of his hands on his unsuccessful attempt to check his swing.
He would make one more out in the ninth, lifting a harmless fly ball to left field off top Brewers southpaw Aaron Ashby.
Once again, he did not address reporters postgame, still yet to speak publicly since before the start of the NLDS.
If the Dodgers were to drop Ohtani from the lineup for Game 3 –– when the Brewers will start left-hander Robert Gasser –– the team would have several potential ways to fill his void at DH.
The most obvious one: rookie sensation Josue De Paula.
The 21-year-old has only logged 45 total big-league plate appearances since being called up straight from double-A back in September, but has reached safely in more than half of them.
That includes a pair of impressive walks as a pinch-hitter in recent days; one that helped set up a game-winning rally in Game 4 of the NL Division Series, and another in an ultimately failed ninth-inning comeback bid in Game 1 of the NLCS on Sunday.
Granted, swapping even a diminished version of Ohtani for someone so inexperienced would undoubtedly be a stunning decision on the surface. And if this series weren’t 2-0 for the Brewers, the calculus would be different.
But right now, De Paula might be just as much of an on-base threat, and (given he is fully healthy) is perhaps an even more likely candidate to potentially slug the ball.
And, at this increasingly dire stage, the Dodgers can ill-afford to risk another empty performance from their biggest star.
If not De Paula, the Dodgers could also use the DH spot to potentially fit October hero, and right-handed hitter, Kiké Hernández back in the lineup, after he was dropped back to the bench for Game 2 in favor of Tommy Edman. Perhaps it could also be a way to get Miguel Rojas in as another extra righty bat, especially while he nurses a back injury he suffered in the NLDS.
None of these scenarios, of course, are what the Dodgers wanted to be contemplating so soon into their World Series three-peat bid.
But suddenly, with the stakes rising higher and Ohtani’s performance trending in the opposite direction, all options might need to be on the table.
The best player in baseball, at least in his current physical condition, might need to be benched.

The Los Angeles Dodgers look to even up the NLCS in Game 2 against the Milwaukee Brewers. Last night, they fell 0-1 in the series after a 2-1 pitching duel.
The Dodgers offense was nearly nonexistent, leaving nine runners on base and going 1-for-6 with RISP.
In today’s 2:00 P.M. PST game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made a lineup change involving their best postseason hitter.
Kiké Hernández Out, Tommy Edman In vs. Brewers
Per Los Angeles Dodgers reporter David Vassegh, Kiké Hernández will sit tonight with Tommy Edman taking his place at second and batting ninth.
In five games this postseason, Edman has yet to record hit.
In Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves, Hernández hit a towering two-run home run ultimately lifting the Dodgers to victory.
Aside from that home run, both Edman and Hernández’s bats have been awfully quiet.
But, the NLCS is where Edman shines. In 2024, he won NLCS MVP. Recording 11 RBIS–tying a franchise record–with a home run, and a .407 batting average which included a hit in each game.
Last year against Milwakuee in the NLCS, Edman tallied five hits and three RBIs.
Tonight, the Dodgers need at least one bat to breakout and shift the momentum of the series before heading home for Games 3 through 5.

Dave Roberts made several slight tweaks aside from the Tommy Edman, Kiké Hernández switch.

Tucker has occupied that lower spot throughout the postse
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers released their lineup for Game 1 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday, and the placement of Kyle Tucker once again drew attention.
Manager Dave Roberts slotted the outfielder eighth in the order despite the presence of right-hander Jacob Misiorowski on the mound for Milwaukee, a matchup that might otherwise favor a left-handed bat higher in the lineup, via Underdog MLB.
Tucker has occupied that lower spot throughout the postseason, including during the Dodgers’ series against the Atlanta Braves.
The decision keeps him in right field while the top of the order features Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base, Will Smith catching, and Shohei Ohtani as the designated hitter batting cleanup. Teoscar Hernández, Max Muncy, and Andy Pages follow before Tucker, with Enrique Hernández handling second base in place of the unavailable Tommy Edman and Miguel Rojas.
Tarik Skubal, acquired from Detroit at the trade deadline, starts for Los Angeles opposite Misiorowski in the series opener at American Family Field.
The arrangement reflects a broader pattern for Tucker in his first season with the Dodgers. After signing a four-year, $240 million contract in free agency, choosing the defending champions over longer offers elsewhere, he posted a .233 batting average with 17 home runs and 70 RBIs across 154 regular-season games.
Those numbers fell short of the production many expected from a player who had delivered multiple 30-home-run seasons earlier in his career. Roberts and the front office have nonetheless kept him in the everyday mix, banking on the October performance that motivated the signing in the first place.
Tucker has shown signs of that form since early September and carried it into the Division Series. He went 5-for-15 with a home run, two RBIs, and two stolen bases against Atlanta, batting .333 in limited action.
Those at-bats included a two-run homer in the series opener at Dodger Stadium.
With the Dodgers seeking a third consecutive World Series appearance, the NLCS against a Brewers club that won 103 games offers the clearest stage yet for the 29-year-old to justify the investment.
A productive stretch against Milwaukee’s pitching staff would quiet questions about his regular-season output and reinforce the club’s bet that his best baseball remains ahead.
For now, the eighth spot keeps Tucker in the lineup without disrupting the balance Roberts has settled on for the series.
Both clubs enter the matchup after efficient Division Series victories, and the early pitching duel between Skubal and Misiorowski sets a high bar for the hitters behind them.
Tucker’s ability to contribute from the lower third of the order will factor into whether Los Angeles can seize an early advantage on the road.

item.title: [New York Post] How the ‘Dinosaur’ Dodgers continue to find the fountain of youth
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: MILWAUKEE –– Dave Roberts delivered the speech. Teoscar Hernández supplied the punch line. In the wake of their National League Division Series defeat of the Atlanta Braves last week, the Dodgers gathered around their manager at the start of a champagne celebration in Truist Park’s visiting clubhouse. First, Roberts extolled their culture and competitiveness. He then declared that “we’re smarter, we’re better and we’re tougher” than their postseason competition. That’s when, from the corner of t
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– Dave Roberts delivered the speech. Teoscar Hernández supplied the punch line.
In the wake of their National League Division Series defeat of the Atlanta Braves last week, the Dodgers gathered around their manager at the start of a champagne celebration in Truist Park’s visiting clubhouse.
First, Roberts extolled their culture and competitiveness. He then declared that “we’re smarter, we’re better and we’re tougher” than their postseason competition.
That’s when, from the corner of the room, Hernández chimed in with one more observation.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” he shouted.
Cretaceous creatures, who have once again found the fountain of October youth.
Throughout the regular season and leading into the playoffs, the Dodgers’ aging roster loomed as their biggest area of concern. Their average lineup age of 30.9 years old, according to Baseball Reference, was the oldest in the majors.
Their grizzled veteran core has played more games (and traveled more miles, including two season-opening Asia trips) than any other club in baseball the past two years.

That’s why the team could help but notice the recent “dinosaur” comment made by new Padres owner José E. Feliciano –– even if he was trying to refer to the actual collection of fossils kept by Dodgers owner Mark Walter.
To the two-time defending champions, it still qualified as a perceived slight.
“We’ve heard it,” 36-year-old third baseman Max Muncy said. “But you can’t focus on the outside stuff for us.
Indeed, the Dodgers do not need any extra motivation this postseason, as they continue their quest for a third-straight World Series title in the NL Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
“You worry about yourself,” Muncy said. “You worry about how you’re getting ready for the game, how you’re preparing for the series.”
But talk about their age has nonetheless added some fuel to their competitive fire.
“Los Viejitos!!!” Kiké Hernández captioned on an Instagram photo of him, Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman earlier this week –– playfully using the Spanish term for “old folks” to describe the club’s five eldest statesmen.
“I like our dinosaurs,” Roberts also joked with AM 570 earlier this month. “Our dinosaurs have come through in the biggest spots.”
That was not always the case during the second half of this year’s regular season, when the Dodgers’ offense slipped into such a glaring funk –– highlighted by an inability to consistently slug the ball –– that one rival scout remarked in late August: “This is the oldest they’ve ever looked.”
Since then, however, they have rediscovered a jolt. They scored the fourth-most runs in the majors in September. They outslugged the Braves in the NLDS by belting eight home runs, all but one of which came from players age 33 or older.
Now, they are banking on their experience to give them an edge in this week’s NLCS, starting with a showdown against 24-year-old flamethrowing Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1 on Sunday.
“The toughest part about age is [managing it during the regular] season,” Roberts said. “But once you get through the marathon and you get to the sprint of the postseason, advantage goes to us in the sense of the experience.”
Father Time, of course, will eventually win out at some point.
Even Muncy acknowledged that there has been “some talk” of this being a potential final ride for this version of the roster.
“For us, it’s about playing for each other, and that’s what makes it so special,” Muncy said. “A lot of us have been through a lot of moments together –– good, bad, in the middle –– and I wouldn’t want to share those with anyone else, that’s for sure.”
For now, however, the Dinosaur Dodgers just want to keep on roaring.
Eight wins away from another World Series, age is the least of their concerns.
“I don’t like thinking that this could be towards the end [of our run], because I don’t think it is,” Muncy said. “I think we still have a lot of good baseball left in us. Hopefully we can keep going.”

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Kiké Hernandez revealed that a minor league player helped fuel Edwin Diaz’s rise.
What caused Edwin Diaz’s turnaround
After Game 4 of the NLDS, amid a wild clubhouse celebration after the NLCS spot was clinched, Kiké Hernandez revealed that minor league catcher Chadwick Tromp found the issue in Diaz’s mechanics.
Tromp signed a minor-league deal with the Dodgers midseason.
“A former Brave, Chadwick Tromp, who was with us in AAA, noticed something in his mechanics, and they went over it after the game, and it was a very easy fix, and Sugar is back to being Sugar,” Hernandez said.
Since returning, the command has been much better for Diaz, while the velocity continues to increase, as does the fastball and slider movement.
Diaz and the Dodgers felt he was a few tweaks away from becoming the guy they signed for $69 million, and they were right.
Edwin Diaz’s full arc
Diaz has turned his debut Dodgers season around since returning from the injured list and a topsy-turvy minor league rehab assignment with the OKC Comets in Triple-A.
After a horrendous season by his standards, Diaz returned on September 18th and hasn’t allowed a run since.
He allowed one hit and a walk over five shutout innings in the regular season, and Dave Roberts trusted him enough to make the postseason roster and give him a high-leverage spot.
In return, Diaz made three appearances in the four-game NLDS, allowing one hard-hit single and recording two saves.
His postseason performance marked a full turnaround for Diaz.
“He’s had a tough season,” Roberts said after the NLDS. “He’s been hurt. He was having trouble with his delivery and went on a long rehab assignment.
“But to get him pitching this way – that’s the reason why we got him. The last two nights, that’s the reason why we acquired a guy like Edwin Diaz.
“He’s one of the great closers in the game. For him to be pitching his best right now, that’s what you hope for, and I give him a lot of credit.”
Now, Diaz is expected to keep closing, or at the very least, play a major role on the closing committee.

Not everything about this Series is the same, though. “I think it is different this year. … We’re going in to beat them,” Murphy told Fox Sports, referring to his team getting swept in 2025. “
item.content:encoded:
Ladies and gentlemen, we’ve got ourselves a rematch.
Just like last year, Shohei Ohtani’s Los Angeles Dodgers and Christian Yelich’s Milwaukee Brewers are meeting in the NLCS.
And, once again, Pat Murphy’s club has home-field advantage. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be at American Family Field in Milwaukee, WI.
Not everything about this Series is the same, though.
“I think it is different this year. … We’re going in to beat them,” Murphy told Fox Sports, referring to his team getting swept in 2025. “We earned it in the regular season to get home-field advantage. We’re going in to beat them, we don’t care who they have.”
If you’d like to be there to see if the Brew Crew really have what it takes to dethrone the defending World Series champion Dodgers, tickets are available for all four hypothetical contests in the Cream City.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on seats for any one game in Milwaukee was $224 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $144 including fees for fans hoping to attend a showdown at Dodger Stadium.
Ahead of the NLCS, Milwaukee battled with San Diego in a tense, back-and-forth four-game NLDS that saw instantly iconic moments like a clutch Jackson Chourio catch in Game 1, a Jackson Chourio walk-off single in Game 2 and Garrett Mitchell robbing Manny Machado of a home run in Game 4.
As for the Dodgers, the club continued their winning ways in the postseason [Editor’s Note: They haven’t lost a playoff series since the Diamondbacks beat them in the 2023 NLDS] and beat up on the formidable Braves.
Kiké Hernández smashed a home run — the 17th postseason dinger of his career, putting him ahead of Babe Ruth (!) on the all-time list — in the decisive fourth game and stellar offensive performances from Andy Pages and Max Muncy.
We can’t wait to see what comes next.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Dodgers vs. Brewers 2026 NLCS below.
What do the cheapest tickets cost for NLCS games in Milwaukee?
A complete breakdown of all the best prices on tickets for every hypothetical game at Milwaukee’s American Family Field can be found here:
| Brewers home game dates | Ticket prices start at |
|---|---|
| Game 1 Sunday, Oct. 11 | $236 (including fees) |
| Game 2 Monday, Oct. 12 | $224 (including fees) |
| Game 6 Sunday, Oct. 18 | $235 (including fees) |
| Game 7 Monday, Oct. 19 | $277 (including fees) |
How much are the cheapest tickets for NLCS games in Los Angeles?
All of the cheapest potential Dodgers NLCS home game ticket prices are listed below.
| Dodgers home game dates | Ticket prices start at |
|---|---|
| Game 3 Wednesday, Oct. 14 | $160 (including fees) |
| Game 4 Thursday, Oct. 15 | $150 (including fees) |
| Game 5 Friday, Oct. 16 | $144 (including fees) |
How can I watch the Dodgers vs. Brewers 2026 NLCS?
For fans who prefer to watch on the tube, you can catch this nervy series on FOX and FS1.
Both providers listed above can be found on the one-stop shop known as DIRECTV.
Huge 2026-27 concerts
Fans hoping to get a concert or three in this year too are in luck.
After a bit of digging, we found that many of the biggest names in music will be on the road this year and next.
Here are just five of the biggest acts and artists we can’t wait to see live in the near future.
• RUSH
Who else is out and about? Take a look at this list of all the biggest rockers on tour in 2026 to find the show for you.
This article was written by Matt Levy, New York Post live events reporter. Levy stays up-to-date on all the latest tour announcements from your favorite musical artists and comedians, as well as Broadway openings, sporting events and more live shows – and finds great ticket prices online. Since he started his tenure at the Post in 2022, Levy has reviewed a Bruce Springsteen concert and interviewed Melissa Villaseñor of SNL fame, to name a few. Please note that deals can expire, and all prices are subject to change.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are headed to the National League Championship Series for the third straight season.
After defeating the Atlanta Braves in four games, the Dodgers will head to Milwaukee to take on the Brewers for a 2nd straight season and potentially advance to the World Series.
LA picked up a 4-1 win over the Braves to advance on Wednesday evening, and immediately following the win, Edwin Diaz, who picked up the save, sent out a 4-word message on social media.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Next Opponent: Who Does LA Play in the NLCS?
Edwin Diaz Sends Message After Advancing to the NLCS
When the Dodgers inked Edwin Diaz to the largest contract for a reliever in MLB history, it was to close out games in October, and considering Diaz picked up saves in both Game Three and Four of the NLDS, it's safe to say he's the team's closer once again.
Via X.com, he had this message to relay after the postgame celebration on Wednesday evening:
@SugarDiaz39: "NLCS LETS GOOO DODGERS"
Edwin Diaz is fired up to be one step away from the World Series, as should the rest of the team.
Diaz struggled for much of the regular season and also battled injuries, but since returning from the IL in late September, he has been lights out.
More MLB on Heavy: Ronald Acuña Jr. Off-Field News Surfaces After Braves-Dodgers NLDS
Looking at Edwin Diaz's First Season with the Los Angeles Dodgers
Edwin Diaz has thrown three innings during the MLB playoffs, and he has yet to allow a run on just one hit allowed and three strikeouts.
During the regular season, Diaz posted an ERA of 8.68 over 18.2 innings.
As noted, the Dodgers inked Diaz to such a lucrative contract to show up when it matters in October, and the 3X All-Star has clearly done that thus far.
Diaz has not allowed a run in his last eight relief outings.
More MLB on Heavy: Kike Hernandez Making MLB History Shouldn't Surprise Los Angeles Dodgers Fans
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Los Angeles Dodgers' Edwin Diaz Sends 4-Word Message After Braves Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: He finally did it! Dodgers' Andy Pages ends two-year postseason slump at the perfect time

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
He pounded his chest twice as he left the batter’s box, and all of Dodgers nation rocked to the beat.
Andy Pages did it. He finally did it. He finally broke out of his baffling two-year October slump with a hit so powerful, he didn’t even have to climb over Kiké Hernández to get it.
How powerful? With one smooth swing he broke a tie by scoring two runs while sending two teams packing, the Atlanta Braves trudging home for the winter and the Dodgers charging into the National League Championship Series.
Yeah, it was a blast, both figuratively and literally, Pages’ two-out, two-strike bases-loaded single in the seventh inning Wednesday night silencing the lame tomahawk-chopping fans at Truist Park and giving the Dodgers an eventual clinching 4-1 victory against the Braves in the National League Division Series.
Certainly, it only gets tougher from here. In winning this best-of-five series three games to one, the Dodgers can now prepare for a best-of-seven showdown task against either the mighty Milwaukee Brewers or blazing San Diego Padres.
Yes, they will need to hit better, they will need Blake Snell to find his focus, they will need Shohei Ohtani to show up.
But…Andy Pages! Seriously! If a guy who was seven for 66 in the last two postseasons and was so helpless last year he was benched for the last three games of the World Series…if that guy can drive in the winning run from the bottom of the order? The once-fallible Dodgers may just be unbeatable.
“There’s no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers,” manager Dave Roberts shouted in the postgame clubhouse. “We’re the best organization in sports, top to bottom. We’re smarter, we’re better, and we’re tougher.”
At that point, someone referenced a recent comment from Padres owner José E. Feliciano insinuating that the Dodgers, baseball’s oldest team, was composed of dinosaurs.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” shouted a voice above the clubhouse din.
If they’re dinosaurs, their first initial is “T” and their last name is ‘Rex.”
It’s OK to start seriously thinking about a three-peat now. They’re now just eight wins away but, given how mediocre the American League playoff teams appear, they could realistically be just four wins away.
Andy Pages comes through in the seventh inning to break a tie and four relievers close out a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves to win the NLDS in four games.
Here’s guessing that the NLCS will be the real World Series. And here’s guessing the Dodgers will be ready.
Pages, who won the hearts of Dodger fans last October when he made a leaping game-saving catch over the back of Kiké Hernández, was granted his first big October swing thanks to the Braves largess.
In the seventh inning of a 1-all tie, Teoscar Hernández redeemed himself for another fielding blunder with a single that finally drove dizzying Tyler Mahle from the game.
In came Game 2 rookie sensation Didier Fuentes, only this time, he was all rookie and zero sensation, walking Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases. Considering De Paula is just a kid and Tucker has been struggling, the fact that both showed such patience in such a pressure situation was pretty cool. And moments later, it got even cooler.
In came veteran reliever Robert Suarez, and Pages was ready for him, working the count full before lining the two-run single up the middle.
The Dodgers added a run two innings later on a Max Muncy home run — has there ever been a playoff game when he hasn’t homered? — to finalize the score.
When the game ended on an Austin Riley fly out to right field, Pages celebrated in center field by taking off his cap, turning his face to the sky and pounding the cap three times into his glove.
It was a series that was worth the emotion, the Dodgers famous starting rotation giving up just four runs in 21 ⅓ innings, the bullpen solid behind a revived Edwin Díaz, and the offense doing just enough to beat Braves aces Chris Sale and Mahle.
In the fifth inning of a tie game, starter Tyler Glasnow issued walks to Riley and Michael Harris II. With two out, in came Alex Vesia. Up stepped slugger Matt Olson. The fans climbed to their feet. This was the Braves’ big chance.
But Olson swung at the first pitch and lined it directly to second baseman Kiké Hernández to end the threat and quiet the joint. Díaz threw a hitless ninth for his second save of the series and…who’s going to beat them?
Afterward, Roberts referenced nearly half of his team when talking about his pride. He talked about Pages’ hit, about De Paula’s walk, about reliever Edgardo Henriquez’s 1 ⅔ shutout innings, about Muncy’s bat and Freddie Freeman’s glove
“I guess, amazement,” he said. “Our guys just continue to fight, persevere. You never know who the guy’s going to be.”
The only glaring weakness was, once again, the superstar who used to be their strength. Ohtani scored the Dodgers’ first run after drawing a walk but went hitless in three ensuing at-bats. He only got two hits in the four-game series and you have to wonder if his injury-wracked body would be better out of the lineup.
How well are they playing without the full services of their most historic player? On the verge of making history, the Dodgers don’t even miss him.
